notes.explains: White's Qh5 attacks e5 but does not defend e4, and the queen becomes a target. Black should develop naturally rather than panic-defend the c5-pawn.
notes.teaches: When the opponent makes an early queen sortie, the best response is often to continue developing with tempo, trusting that the queen will become vulnerable.
notes.plans: Develop Nf6, attacking the queen and preparing to occupy the center with d5 or e6.

notes.explains: Bc4 threatens checkmate on f7. The best defense is e6, which blocks the bishop but prepares a solid pawn center with d5. The light-squared bishop may be passive on d7, but that is acceptable.
notes.teaches: Not every piece needs to be active immediately. A temporarily passive bishop is a small price to pay for a safe king and a strong center.
notes.plans: Play e6, then d5, followed by Bc5 (attacking f2) and castling kingside.

notes.explains: White's d3 is a mistake because it allows Nd4, forking the queen and bishop. The queen on f3 is vulnerable, and Nd4 creates multiple threats.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is exposed, look for forks and double attacks that exploit its vulnerability.
notes.plans: Play Nd4, threatening Nxc2+ and the bishop on b5. After Qd1, capture the bishop with Nxb5, winning a pawn and maintaining pressure.

notes.explains: Nc3 develops with tempo, attacking the queen. This highlights the fundamental weakness of the Scandinavian: Black moves the queen multiple times, falling behind in development.
notes.teaches: Develop with tempo whenever possible. Punish early queen moves by gaining time and central control.
notes.plans: After Qe6+, block with Be2, then play Nf3, d4, and castle kingside, building a massive lead in development.

notes.explains: Black's Bd7 is a serious mistake because it does nothing to address the development deficit. White can now play Nf3, d4, and castle, while Black's queen remains a target.
notes.teaches: In the opening, every move should either develop a piece, control the center, or improve king safety. Wasting time with passive moves like Bd7 is fatal.
notes.plans: Play Nf3, then d4 (threatening d5 forking queen and knight), castle, and exploit Black's undeveloped kingside.

notes.explains: d4 threatens d5, forking the queen on e6 and the knight on c6. Black's queen has no good square: Qd6 loses to Nb5, and Qg6 allows d5 with a strong attack.
notes.teaches: A pawn fork in the center can be devastating when the opponent's pieces are poorly coordinated. Always look for such tactical opportunities.
notes.plans: Push d5, winning material or forcing a decisive positional concession. If Black plays Qd6, Nb5 wins the queen. If Qg6, continue with d5 and develop with tempo.

notes.explains: Black's e5 is a blunder that loses a piece. White can capture with Nxe5 or Qxd4, both winning. Qxd4 is especially strong because it prevents queenside castling and threatens Qxa7.
notes.teaches: When you have a huge lead in development, look for direct tactical blows. A single mistake by the opponent can end the game immediately.
notes.plans: Capture on d4 with the queen, then play Bf4 to cover c7 and threaten checkmate on a8 or b8. Black's king is trapped.

notes.explains: Bf4 covers c7, threatening checkmate on a8 and b8. Black's king is trapped, and the only way to avoid immediate mate is to sacrifice the queen with Qd6.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed and your pieces are active, look for mating nets. Covering escape squares is often more important than material.
notes.plans: Play Bf4, threatening Qa8# and Qb8#. If Black plays Qd6, capture it and win easily.

notes.explains: When Black plays ...Nc6, White should immediately play c4 to challenge the knight on d5, rather than castling first. Delaying c4 allows Black to take on d4 and develop with ...Nc6, making c4 less effective.
notes.teaches: Meet central challenges directly; don't give the opponent time to complete development before striking.
notes.plans: After c4, if the knight moves, continue with Nc3 and development.

notes.explains: If Black plays ...Nb4, White can simply play a3, chasing the knight. This is not dangerous because the bishop on e2 prevents the fork on c2.
notes.teaches: Don't fear knight jumps if you have a simple refutation; a3 gains time and space.
notes.plans: After a3, the knight retreats; continue developing with Nc3.

notes.explains: After …cxd5, White recaptures with the knight (Nxd5), not the queen, to avoid ...Nc6 attacking the queen. Keeping the queen centralized is less important than avoiding tempos.
notes.teaches: Recapture with the piece that doesn't walk into a developing move by the opponent.
notes.plans: After Nxd5, Black may play ...Nc6; White continues with development and prepares d5.

notes.explains: Now d5 is a strong tempo move, attacking the knight and preventing Black from playing ...Bd6 to blockade the passed pawn. The pawn becomes a powerful asset.
notes.teaches: A passed pawn is only strong if it cannot be blockaded; use tempo to deny the opponent the chance to blockade.
notes.plans: Follow with Bf4 to prevent ...Bd6, then continue development.

notes.explains: Bf4 prevents ...Bd6 and develops the bishop to an active square. If Black plays ...Bd6 anyway, the pawn on d5 supports Bf4, and the bishop is nearly trapped.
notes.teaches: Use your pawns to restrict the opponent's pieces; a passed pawn can also support your own pieces.
notes.plans: After Bf4, prepare to castle and bring the rook to d1.

notes.explains: After ...Bd6, White trades bishops, leaving Black with a weak dark-square complex and the passed pawn on d5 still strong. Black's queen on d6 is also exposed.
notes.teaches: Trading off a blockading piece can strengthen your passed pawn.
notes.plans: Castle, then bring the rook to d1 to pressure the queen and pawn.

notes.explains: Castling is better than playing a3 to kick the bishop on b4. a3 would take away the a3 square from White's dark-squared bishop, which could be a useful developing post if Black later takes on c3.
notes.teaches: Avoid unnecessary pawn moves that might deprive your pieces of good squares; develop with maximum flexibility.
notes.plans: After castling, continue with Rad1 and consider Bg5 to pin the knight.

notes.explains: Bg5 pins the knight on f6, which is very dangerous for Black because the queen is also on the same diagonal. The threat of Nxg4 or d6 is strong.
notes.teaches: Pins are especially powerful when the pinned piece is defending the king or other important squares.
notes.plans: If Black plays ...h6, consider Bxf6 to open the g-file, or retreat to h4 to maintain the pin.

notes.explains: If Black weakens the kingside with ...g5, White retreats the bishop to g3, keeping the pressure. Black's pawn moves create permanent weaknesses.
notes.teaches: Provoke pawn weaknesses that compromise the opponent's king safety; the weaknesses will be exploitable later.
notes.plans: Continue with Rad1, preparing d6 or other breaks.

notes.explains: Rad1 is a crushing move: it threatens d6 (winning the bishop on d7) and also x-rays the queen. If Black plays ...Bc6, White can simply take on c7 because the queen on d4 is defended by the rook.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are tied down, a simple rook move can create multiple threats. Concrete calculation must override general principles like 'connect pawns'.
notes.plans: After Rad1, Black is defenseless; White will win material by d6 or Bxf6.

notes.explains: Bxf6 is strong because after ...gxf6, the g-file opens, allowing Qd6–g3+ with a discovered check on the queen. The combination wins material.
notes.teaches: Sacrificing a bishop to open a file can create a devastating discovered attack. Always look for ways to combine threats.
notes.plans: After ...gxf6, play Qg3+ to win the queen, then capture the rook.

notes.explains: Qg3+ is a discovered check that wins the queen on d8. The rook on d1 x-rays the queen, and the bishop on c6 cannot defend.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is on the same file as your rook, a discovered check can win it.
notes.plans: After the queen is captured, take the rook on c7 and then the bishop.

notes.explains: After Qg3+ Kh8, White captures the queen on d6, and the rook on c7 is now undefended. Next move, White wins the rook and then the bishop.
notes.teaches: A forced sequence of captures can win multiple pieces; always check if the opponent's pieces are left hanging.
notes.plans: Take the rook on c7, then the bishop on c6.

notes.explains: Nb5 attacks the rook on c7 and threatens Qg3+ again. The rook is overloaded, defending the bishop and the king.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's heavy pieces are tied to defense, a knight fork or discovered attack can decide the game.
notes.plans: If the rook moves, capture the bishop; if not, Nb5 wins the exchange.

notes.explains: Black's rook moves to c8, but White simply captures the bishop on c6, winning a piece. The combination is complete.
notes.teaches: After a successful combination, simplify to a winning endgame.
notes.plans: Trade queens and win the endgame with an extra piece.

notes.explains: Black castles, walking into a classic Greek Gift sacrifice. White can play Bxh7+ followed by Ng5+, Qh5, etc., leading to a winning attack.
notes.teaches: The Greek Gift sacrifice is a standard attacking motif when the bishop is on d3 and the knight can reach g5. It exploits the weakened kingside after castling.
notes.plans: Execute Bxh7+ Kxh7, Ng5+ Kg6 (or Kg8), Qg4, etc., with a mating attack.

notes.explains: White recaptures on d4, and Black's bishop on c8 remains hemmed in. White has a small but lasting advantage due to superior piece activity and Black's bad bishop.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, a bad bishop can be a decisive weakness. White should aim to keep the position closed and exploit Black's lack of space.
notes.plans: Play c3 to support the bishop, then develop the queenside with b3 and Bb2, gradually increasing pressure.

notes.explains: Black plays Qb6, attacking the b2 pawn and preparing to support the queenside pawns. White should respond with a4 to break up Black's pawn chain.
notes.teaches: When Black builds a queenside pawn chain (b5, c4), White can undermine it with b3 and a4. The timing is critical: a4 is strong when the rook on a8 is undefended.
notes.plans: Play a4 immediately, exploiting the undefended rook on a8. If Black plays ...a6, then axb5 axb5? loses the rook. This forces Black to defend passively.

notes.explains: White plays a4, threatening to break the queenside pawn chain. Black cannot play ...a6 because axb5 axb5? loses the rook. This forces Black to defend with a piece.
notes.teaches: A pawn break like a4 can be devastating when the opponent's rook is undefended. The threat of winning a pawn or exposing weaknesses forces concessions.
notes.plans: After a4, if Black plays ...Ba6, White can capture on b5 and c4, leaving Black with a weak pawn on c4. Then White will target that pawn with Rb1, Qe2, etc.

notes.explains: White clears the queenside pawns, leaving Black with a weak isolated pawn on c4. White now has a clear target and better piece activity.
notes.teaches: Exchanging pawns to create a permanent weakness (isolated pawn) is a key strategic idea. The c4 pawn is a long-term liability for Black.
notes.plans: White will complete development (c3, Nbd2, Rc1, etc.) and then surround and win the c4 pawn. Black cannot easily defend it.

notes.explains: White plays c3 to solidify the center and prepares Nbd2 to target the c4 pawn. Black's rook on d8 does not threaten d4 because the knight on f3 guards it.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, solidifying the center with c3 is often necessary before pursuing a queenside plan. The knight on f3 is a key defender.
notes.plans: White will play Nbd2, then perhaps Ne4 or Nf1-e3 to pressure c4. The c4 pawn is a fixed target that cannot be easily defended.

notes.explains: Black plays f6, challenging the e5 pawn and opening the center. White must reassess: the plan to target c4 is now secondary to exploiting the new weakness on e6.
notes.teaches: Flexibility is crucial. When the opponent changes the structure, be ready to switch plans. Here, the opening of the center favors the better-developed side (White).
notes.plans: White should capture on f6 (exf6), opening the e-file and targeting the weak e6 pawn. Then Qe2 or Rfe1 puts pressure on e6.

notes.explains: White captures on f6 and plays Rfe1, putting pressure on e6. Black's king is still in the center, and the e6 pawn is a major weakness.
notes.teaches: After opening the center, the side with better development should target the opponent's weak pawns. The rook on e1 adds pressure and prepares to double on the e-file.
notes.plans: White will play Qe2 or Qd3, attacking e6. Black cannot easily defend it because the king is exposed and pieces are undeveloped.

notes.explains: Black plays Kf7 to defend e6, but this is a decisive mistake. White can now play Ng5+, forcing the king back or to a worse square.
notes.teaches: The king is a poor defender in open positions. Moving it forward often creates new tactical opportunities for the opponent.
notes.plans: Play Ng5+ Ke7 (or Kg8), then capture on e6 with the rook or knight, winning a pawn and exposing the king further.

notes.explains: White plays d5, winning the knight on c6 because the queen on b6 is pinned to the king. Black's position collapses immediately.
notes.teaches: A pin can be decisive. Here, the queen's pin on the knight allows a simple pawn advance to win material and launch a mating attack.
notes.plans: After d5, Black cannot avoid losing the knight. White will then deliver checkmate with Qd4+ and Bf4, or similar.

notes.explains: White delivers checkmate with Qxd6#. The game is a clear example of converting a positional advantage into a direct attack.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed and pieces are undeveloped, a coordinated attack can end the game quickly. Accurate calculation of forcing moves is essential.
notes.plans: The mating sequence is forced: d5 wins the knight, then Qxd5+ forces the king to c7, and Bf4+ Bd6 Qxd6#.

notes.explains: This game illustrates key ideas of the Nimzowitsch French: rapid development, undermining the queenside pawn chain, flexibility in switching plans, and exploiting the opponent's king exposure.
notes.teaches: The Nimzowitsch French is a practical weapon that teaches closed position strategy, pawn breaks, and attacking chess. It is effective up to a high level.

notes.explains: After both kings move to b1 and b8, White's next step is to trade off Black's strongest piece: the bishop on e5. Bf4 is a good move because it exchanges a powerful bishop for a passive one, and the tactics work (Nxd4 is impossible due to pin).
notes.teaches: Trading your opponent's best piece is a key positional idea. Here, the bishop on e5 controls many squares; removing it leaves Black with a bad bishop on e6.
notes.plans: Play Bf4, then after the trade, bring the rook to e1 to pressure the e6 bishop, and continue improving pieces.

notes.explains: After the bishop trade, White has a pleasant position. The next step is to bring the rook to e1, putting pressure on the e6 bishop. Black's pieces are passive, and White can continue accumulating pressure.
notes.teaches: When you have a positional advantage, keep making improving moves. Bring rooks to open files, target weak pieces, and avoid rushing. The opponent will eventually run out of good moves.
notes.plans: Play Rde1, then consider tactical ideas like Bxe6 followed by Qd6 trade, exploiting the alignment of rooks on the d-file.

notes.explains: Black plays Qd6, offering a queen trade. White can transform the positional advantage into a tactical one by noticing the alignment of rooks on the d-file and the undefended rook on d6. The sequence Bxe6 (defending the queen), then Qxd6, then Nxe6 exploits this.
notes.teaches: When all your pieces are on perfect squares, look for tactics. Here, the undefended rook on d6 and the alignment of heavy pieces create a tactical opportunity. Don't be afraid to change the pawn structure to shift the target of attack.
notes.plans: Play Bxe6, then Qxd6, then Nxe6, winning a pawn. The resulting endgame is winning due to the weak e6 pawn and active pieces.

notes.explains: After Nxe6, White has won a pawn. The knight on e6 is strong, controlling d8 and attacking the d5 pawn. Black's pieces are passive. White's plan is to consolidate and win more pawns.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, keep your rooks on open files and use your knight to create threats. Avoid tunneling on one weakness; look for ways to create multiple threats.
notes.plans: Play Ba4 (to later go to b3, attacking d5), then c3 to immobilize d5, and eventually win the d5 pawn. If Black tries counterplay, use tactics like Ng7 to fork rooks.

notes.explains: After …Nb4, White has a winning tactic: Ng7 forks the rooks. This move is easy to miss because the knight goes to an unusual square (g7), but it exploits the undefended rook on e8 and the pinned knight on e7.
notes.teaches: Avoid tunnel vision on one plan (e.g., winning the d5 pawn). Look for geometric moves like knight forks. When your pieces are well-placed, always check for tactical blows that win material immediately.
notes.plans: Play Ng7, winning the exchange. After that, use the extra material to win the game.

notes.explains: After e5 c3 Nc6 cxd4 exd4, White can play Bc4, transposing to an Alapin line. Black should play Nf6, and if White plays Ng5, Black has the defensive resource Qb4+ to enable castling and protect f7.
notes.teaches: In Fried Liver-type attacks, a queen check can be a unique defensive resource to get the king to safety.
notes.plans: Play Nf6, and if Ng5, Qb4+ followed by O-O.

notes.explains: Black has many good setups (e6, d6, g6, a6) depending on one's preferred Sicilian variation. Here, the fianchetto (g6) is chosen as it fits the Accelerated Dragon style.
notes.teaches: Choose your setup based on the type of Sicilian you play; consistency helps in understanding typical plans.
notes.plans: Develop with g6, Bg7, and later consider d5 to open the center.

notes.explains: Bd2 intends Bc3 to pressure the kingside, but Black should not trade bishops; instead, continue development.
notes.teaches: Avoid trading your fianchettoed bishop for a less active piece; it is a key defender.
notes.plans: Continue with Bg7, Nf6, and castle, preparing to open the center with d5.

notes.explains: c3 is a poor move because it does not develop and restricts White's knight; White's lack of development is becoming critical.
notes.teaches: Avoid unnecessary pawn moves that hinder your own pieces; prioritize development.
notes.plans: Black continues developing normally, aiming to open the center soon.

notes.explains: Nf6 is chosen over e6 and Bg7 because here rapid development and opening the center are more important than preserving the fianchetto bishop's diagonal. The d6 square is also a concern.
notes.teaches: Prioritize development speed over rigid setup when the center is fluid; sometimes a knight on f6 is more active than a pawn on e6.
notes.plans: Castle next, then prepare d5 to open the center.

notes.explains: Black castles, completing development and ensuring king safety before pushing d5.
notes.teaches: Always secure your king before launching central operations, especially when the opponent is underdeveloped.
notes.plans: Now ready to play d5, opening the center while White is still undeveloped.

notes.explains: e5 is a terrible move for White, overextending without development. Black's knight should go to d5, keeping central control, though Nh5 is also possible.
notes.teaches: When a pawn advances, look for the square it vacates and consider occupying it with a piece.
notes.plans: Play Nd5, centralizing the knight and preparing further pressure.

notes.explains: White's queen on e4 is vulnerable. Black should take the e5 pawn with the knight (Nxe5), not the bishop, because Nxe5 threatens a fork on d3 and keeps the queen exposed.
notes.teaches: When capturing, consider which piece leaves the opponent's queen most vulnerable; avoid moving your bishop from its strong diagonal without good reason.
notes.plans: Play Nxe5, threatening Nd3+ and winning the queen.

notes.explains: Black chooses Qc7 over Qb6. Qc7 is not just a threat (Nd3+ wins queen) but also useful if White castles queenside (x-rays c3) and helps coordinate rooks.
notes.teaches: A good move should be useful even without the immediate threat; avoid 'one-move-tricks' that have no follow-up.
notes.plans: Play Qc7, threatening Nd3+ and preparing further development.

notes.explains: Nd3+ forks king and queen, winning the queen. White's lack of development made this possible.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is exposed and the king is vulnerable, look for forks and discoveries.
notes.plans: Win the queen and convert the material advantage.

notes.explains: After winning the queen, Black is up massive material. Instead of grabbing more material (Qxf2), Black should open the center with d5 to exploit White's poor development.
notes.teaches: When ahead in material, prioritize opening lines and activating pieces over grabbing more pawns; speed up the attack.
notes.plans: Play d5, opening the d-file and bringing the rook to d8, targeting the knight on d2.

notes.explains: Black plays d5, sacrificing a pawn to open the d-file. The rook will go to d8, and the bishop can go to h6 to target the knight on d2.
notes.teaches: Sacrificing material to accelerate the attack is often correct when the opponent is undeveloped.
notes.plans: Play Rd8, then Bh6, and look for ways to eliminate the knight on d2.

notes.explains: Black must be careful: after Bh6, if White plays Kb1, the knight on f3 can be captured but the d2 knight recaptures. So Black should play Bf5 first, preventing Kb1 and preparing Rc8 with mate threats.
notes.teaches: When attacking, prevent the opponent's king from escaping; a moving target is harder to hit.
notes.plans: Play Bf5, then Rc8, threatening sacrifices on c3 and a hidden mate threat.

notes.explains: Black has a hidden mate threat: Qe4, threatening Qb1# because the knight on d2 is pinned to the king. The knight cannot capture the queen.
notes.teaches: Always consider pins; a piece that appears to defend a square may be immobilized. If you see a good move (like taking the free knight), look for a better one (like Qe4 with mate threat).
notes.plans: Play Qe4, threatening Qb1#. White's only defense is Re1, but then Black can win material or checkmate.

notes.explains: If White had played correctly (Nf3, Nc3, Be2, O-O), the position would be close to equal. But White's inaccuracies (Bd2, c3, e5) gave Black a clear advantage.
notes.teaches: Even after a poor opening, accurate development can keep the balance; one must not panic.
notes.plans: Black should continue developing and look to open the center.

notes.explains: If White plays Bc3, Black should not fear it. Nd5 is a strong response, pressuring the bishop. If White takes on d5, Black recaptures with the knight and can 'castle by hand' (Rf8, Kg8) to safety.
notes.teaches: When your king is exposed, you can often 'castle artificially' by moving the rook and king manually. Don't fear exchanges that open lines if you have active pieces.
notes.plans: Play Nd5, and if Bxd5, exd5, then Rf8, Kg8, and later d5.

notes.explains: After artificial castling, Black is safe and can push d5. If White plays e5, Black has Ng4 winning the e5 pawn. If exd5, Nxd5 gives Black a massive initiative with potential sacrifices on c3.
notes.teaches: Once the king is safe, open the center to exploit your lead in development.
notes.plans: Play d5, and if e5, Ng4 wins the pawn; if exd5, Nxd5 with strong attack.

notes.explains: If White plays e5, Black should play Ng4, attacking the e5 pawn three times against one defender. This wins the pawn.
notes.teaches: Count attackers and defenders before capturing; if you have more attackers, you win the pawn.
notes.plans: Play Ng4, winning the e5 pawn.

notes.explains: After exd5, Nxd5 gives Black a powerful knight in the center. Black can then play Bf5, and if White plays Nf3, Black can push e5-e4-e3, collapsing White's position.
notes.teaches: A centralized knight supported by pawns can be devastating; use pawn advances to restrict the opponent's pieces.
notes.plans: Play Bf5, then e5, e4, e3, or consider sacrifices on c3.

notes.explains: If White plays Bg3, Black should not play Nxe5? because of Qb5 skewering the knights. Instead, Black should first take on c3? No, the correct move is to create a double attack: Qe4, attacking both undefended pieces (knight on d5 and bishop on g3). The knight cannot defend the bishop because it's on a light square.
notes.teaches: When you see two undefended pieces, look for a fork or double attack. Be aware of skewers and pins that might defend them.
notes.plans: Play Qe4, forking the knight and bishop.

notes.explains: If Black blunders with Nxe5, White has Qb5 skewering the knights. But Black can save the game by creating a counter-threat: Qb6 attacking b2. If White takes the knight, Black takes the rook. This shows the importance of counterplay when behind.
notes.teaches: When you blunder, look for counter-threats using your lead in development or active pieces. Don't panic; find the best move.
notes.plans: Play Qb6, threatening Qxb2 and creating complications.

notes.explains: After Qb6, if White plays Qxe5, Black has Qxb2, winning the rook. White may have compensation but Black is not losing. This is better than panicking and giving up the knight.
notes.teaches: Always look for ways to create threats that force the opponent to defend, rather than accepting material loss.
notes.plans: Play Qb6, and if Qxe5, Qxb2 with counterplay.

notes.explains: After Nc7+ Rxc7 Bxc7, White is up a rook and has a winning position. The game is effectively over. Black's position collapsed due to passive defense and lack of development.
notes.teaches: When you are a pawn up and have the initiative, don't let up. Keep creating threats and forcing concessions. Black's attempt to defend passively (Nd5) only made things worse.
notes.plans: Finish the game by developing the remaining pieces and converting the material advantage.

notes.explains: After Bc4, Black's knight on c5 attacks e3. White can sacrifice the c5 pawn with h3, leading to a complex position where White's light-square control and pawn majority give an advantage.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it's worth giving back the extra pawn to gain positional trumps: bishop pair, light-square control, and a mobile pawn majority. Compare pawn majorities to assess the position.
notes.plans: Play h3, and if Black takes on c5, continue with g4, then develop the knight to d2 or c4. Push the queenside pawns (a4, b4) to create a passed pawn.

notes.explains: After h3, Black cannot take on g2 because of the open lines. White's plan is to keep the bishop pair and push the queenside pawns. The knight on c6 is restricted by the pawns on b4 and c5.
notes.teaches: In positions with a pawn majority, avoid blockading your own pawns. Push the unopposed pawn first (a4 before b5) to prevent the opponent's knight from blocking.
notes.plans: Play a4, then b4, gaining space. If Black plays a5, then b5 is bad because of Na5 blockading. Instead, push a5 first to soften up the knight on c6.

notes.explains: The final sequence shows a classic winning attack. White's pieces coordinate perfectly: the bishop on h3 (via g3) controls c8, the rook on d1 pins the knight, and the knight on b5 delivers the final blow.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development and the opponent's king is stuck in the center, look for tactical blows like Nc7+ that win material. The bishop on h3 is crucial for preventing the king's escape.
notes.plans: Convert the material advantage by developing the remaining pieces and avoiding counterplay.

notes.explains: Black plays Qg5, threatening Qxg2 mate and also preventing White from taking on e4 because of the fork on g2. This forces White to deal with the threat.
notes.teaches: When a knight is on e4, Qg5 can be a powerful move that creates multiple threats and ties down White's pieces.
notes.plans: After Qg5, Black threatens Qxg2# and also prepares to bring the rook to f6 or h6 for a mating attack.

notes.explains: After Kh1, Black can deliver checkmate with Nxg3+ followed by Rf6 and Rh6. White cannot prevent it; even giving up the rook on f2 only delays the mate.
notes.teaches: This is a classic mating pattern: a knight sacrifice on g3 opens the h-file, and the rook swings over to deliver mate. White's king is trapped.
notes.plans: Execute the mate: Nxg3+, hxg3, Rf6, and Rh6#.

notes.explains: The Nimzo-Indian is not just a positional opening; it can lead to powerful attacks, especially with the setup shown (knight on e4, queen on g5, rook lift to h6).
notes.teaches: The Nimzo-Indian is a gateway to sharp attacks. Knowing typical attacking patterns (like the one with Qg5 and Rf6-h6) can lead to brilliant wins.

notes.explains: If White avoids the immediate mate with a move like Nf3, Black can still maintain pressure. The key is to keep the knight on e4 and build up the attack.
notes.teaches: Do not be lulled into creating a threat just because it's tempting; always calculate. In this position, taking on e4 with the knight would allow Bc4, giving White a good knight vs bad bishop scenario.

notes.explains: In the line where White plays d5, Black should recapture with the bishop, not the knight, to avoid a bad bishop vs good knight scenario. The knight on e4 is a strong outpost.
notes.teaches: When choosing between captures, consider the resulting piece quality. A knight outpost is often worth more than a bishop, so keep the knight and trade the bishop.

notes.explains: If White avoids the mate with a move like Nf3, Black can still maintain pressure. The key is to keep the knight on e4 and build up the attack.
notes.teaches: In positions with a knight on e4, look for ways to bring the rook to the kingside (e.g., Rf6-h6) and combine with queen and bishop for a mating attack.

notes.explains: Black now has the queen on f6. White plays Nh5, attacking the queen. Black can safely take the pawn on b2: after Qxb2 Rb1, the queen retreats to e5, where it is safe because f4 would weaken White's pawns and allow Qxe3+.
notes.teaches: Taking a pawn with the queen requires concrete calculation. Here Qxb2 is safe because the queen has a good retreat square (e5) and White's counterplay is insufficient.
notes.plans: After Qe5, Black is up a pawn with a strong position. Black should aim to consolidate, possibly by castling and developing the light-squared bishop.

notes.explains: Black plays Qd4, a strong central square. The queen is safe here because White cannot easily attack it. It also prevents White from castling, as Bxg3 would win a piece due to the pin on f2.
notes.teaches: A centralized queen can be very powerful if it is not easily attacked. Here Qd4 ties White down and prevents castling, creating a decisive advantage.
notes.plans: Black's next moves can include pushing the a-pawn or playing Rfd8 to prepare e5. White's king is stuck in the center and Black's pieces are more active.

notes.explains: White's c4 creates a permanent hole on d4, as neither the c- nor e-pawn can defend it. This gives Black long-term dark-square control.
notes.teaches: A hole is a square that cannot be defended by any pawn. Such weaknesses are strategic targets, especially once development is complete.
notes.plans: Exploit the d4 outpost later, after developing pieces. Do not rush to occupy it immediately.

notes.explains: Playing g6 here allows White to push d4 and transpose to a Maroczy Bind, which is theoretically fine but not the most punishing response. A more critical move is e6 or Nf6, pressuring e4 and preventing d4.
notes.teaches: When White plays c4 early, Black should consider preventing d4 to avoid the Maroczy Bind, which is comfortable for White. Punish the c4 move by targeting e4.
notes.plans: If White plays d4, accept the transposition; if White plays d3, Black gets a comfortable advantage.

notes.explains: Trading the light-squared bishop for the knight on f3 increases Black's control over d4. The knight on f3 is a key defender of d4; removing it makes d4 even more accessible.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, trading a bishop for a knight that defends a key square can be a good strategic exchange, even if it costs a tempo.
notes.plans: After the trade, consider developing the g8-knight to e7 (the 'Botvinnik setup') to avoid obstructing the dark-squared bishop's control of d4.

notes.explains: Developing the knight to e7 rather than f6 keeps the dark-squared bishop's diagonal unobstructed and adds pawn control over d5 and f5. The closed center makes e6 and g6 safe together.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, the rule against playing both e6 and g6 does not apply because the center is blocked. The knight on e7 is a flexible, non-obstructing square.
notes.plans: Complete kingside development with castling, then prepare the queenside pawn break b5.

notes.explains: Playing h6 before castling prevents White from playing Qd2 and Bh6, which would trade off Black's powerful dark-squared bishop. If White takes on e7, Black recaptures with the queen to keep the knight on e7.
notes.teaches: Prevent the exchange of your fianchettoed bishop by provoking a bishop trade on e7 or by preemptively moving the rook. The dark-squared bishop is often the most valuable piece in such structures.
notes.plans: After castling, focus on the queenside pawn break b5.

notes.explains: Black has completed development with a clear advantage: dark-square control, a bad bishop for White, and a flexible pawn structure. The position is roughly -1.5 to -2.
notes.teaches: Recognize when you have a strategic advantage: superior piece activity, control of key squares, and a target (White's bad bishop).
notes.plans: Start converting the advantage by preparing the queenside pawn break b5, often preceded by a6.

notes.explains: The plan is to play b5, opening the queenside and exploiting White's poorly placed queen on a4. a6 prepares b5 and also prevents any tactical tricks.
notes.teaches: In anti-Sicilian structures (non-open Sicilians), the b5 pawn break is a standard plan to open files and create threats against White's queen.
notes.plans: Play b5, and if White captures, recapture with the a-pawn to open the a-file. If White retreats the queen, follow up with Nd4.

notes.explains: Playing Nd4 first is more flexible than b5 immediately. It forces White's bishop to d1 (the only safe square), after which b5 traps the queen on a4.
notes.teaches: When a plan involves a pawn break, consider if a preparatory piece move can improve the timing or create additional threats.
notes.plans: After Nd4 Bd1, play b5, trapping the queen. If White plays Qd1 instead, then b5 is still strong.

notes.explains: b5 traps the queen on a4. White's queen has no safe retreat: d1 is occupied, c2 and b3 are attacked by the knight, and a3 allows b4 forking queen and knight.
notes.teaches: A pawn break can directly win material when the opponent's pieces are poorly placed. Always look for ways to trap or attack the opponent's most active piece.
notes.plans: After b5, White's queen is lost. Capture it or force a favorable trade.

notes.explains: After b5, White's queen escapes to a5. Instead of rushing to trap it with Nc6 (which allows Qb6), play Rfb8 first, defending b6 and threatening Nc6 next move.
notes.teaches: Use 'second-order threats' – moves that set up a decisive threat without being direct. This forces the opponent to deal with the setup, often losing time.
notes.plans: After Rfb8, White cannot prevent Nc6, which will trap the queen. If White plays Ne2 to open a path, Black can play bxc4 or other winning moves.

notes.explains: Black wins the b2-pawn, gaining material and destroying White's queenside. The queen is now active and White's position is hopeless.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, continue to improve your pieces and take free material. Simplify only when it helps, not just for the sake of it.
notes.plans: Activate the queen (e.g., Qg5 threatening Nf3+ and Qd2) and take all remaining pawns.

notes.explains: Qg5 threatens Nf3+ (winning the queen) and Qd2 (forking rook and b2-pawn). White cannot defend both threats.
notes.teaches: When converting an advantage, look for the most active square for your queen. Threats that combine check and material gain are especially powerful.
notes.plans: After White's reply, capture the rook on c1 and then take all remaining pawns.

notes.explains: Black has won a queen for a rook and is up massive material. The remaining plan is to take all of White's pawns and promote.
notes.teaches: In a winning endgame, continue to take free material and avoid unnecessary risks. Simplify only when it speeds up the win.
notes.plans: Capture the a-pawn, then push the queenside pawns to promote.

notes.explains: Black's setup with d6 and e6 creates 'hooks'—pawns that White can dynamite by advancing d5, opening the e-file and exposing Black's king.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a cramped center with pawns on d6 and e6, advancing d5 is a typical way to open lines and punish slow development.
notes.plans: Play d5 to open the center; if Black captures, recapture and continue development.

notes.explains: Black's …Nc6 is a mistake because it mixes two strategies (French and ...c5). The knight on c6 becomes vulnerable to d5 later.
notes.teaches: In the French, Black should play ...d5 and develop normally. Mixing setups like ...Nc6 without ...d5 gives White a free center.
notes.plans: White continues development and prepares d5 to open the center.

notes.explains: After d5 exd5 exd5, Black's best move is ...Ne5, sacrificing a pawn to complete kingside development and castle, rather than ...Nb4 which loses a piece.
notes.teaches: When in a bad position, prioritize king safety and development over material. Sacrificing a pawn to castle is often worth it.
notes.plans: Black should play ...Ne5, then ...Be7, ...O-O, and ...Bd6 to activate the bishop.

notes.explains: Black retreats the knight to f6, defending g7. White plays c4, pushing pawns in the center. Black must avoid e6, which would allow d6 and c5, giving White a strong pawn chain.
notes.teaches: When facing a pawn roller, avoid blocking the center with your pawns if it allows the opponent to advance further. Instead, consider fianchettoing to keep the center flexible.
notes.plans: Black should play g6, fianchettoing the bishop, and then castle. This keeps the e7 pawn in place and prepares to challenge White's center later.

notes.explains: Black plays g6, preparing Bg7. White may consider Bxf6, but that would concede the dark squares and allow Black to open the e-file with ...exf6. Black is not afraid of this because White has no rook on e1 yet.
notes.teaches: Sometimes giving up the bishop pair is acceptable if it leads to other advantages, like opening lines or weakening the opponent's structure.
notes.plans: Black will play Bg7, castle, and then challenge White's center with moves like e6 or b5, depending on how White proceeds.

notes.explains: White plays Be2, a passive move that allows Black to complete development. Black should now play Bg7 and castle, ignoring White's threats on the kingside.
notes.teaches: When the opponent wastes time with slow moves, accelerate your development. Don't be distracted by threats that can be easily parried.
notes.plans: Black castles, then looks to undermine White's center with moves like e6 or b5. The pawn on b4 is a long-term asset.

notes.explains: Both sides castle. Black is up a pawn and has a solid position. White's center looks imposing, but Black has counterplay. White's knight is stuck on b1, which is a major problem.
notes.teaches: A lead in development and an extra pawn can compensate for a seemingly strong enemy center. Look for ways to challenge the center with piece play.
notes.plans: Black can play e6, challenging the d5 square, or b5, attacking the base of White's pawn chain. The knight on b1 is a liability for White.

notes.explains: White plays g4, a reckless attacking move that weakens the kingside. Black should not panic with h6, which only helps White open the h-file. Instead, Black should continue development and ignore the threat.
notes.teaches: When the opponent attacks on the wing, counter in the center or continue your own plans. Don't make reactive pawn moves that create weaknesses.
notes.plans: Black can simply castle (if not already) or play a move like Nf5, preparing to challenge White's center. The g4 pawn is a weakness White will regret.

notes.explains: Black plays Nf5, eyeing d4 and putting pressure on White's center. White's g4 pawn is now a target. Black is not afraid of g5 because the knight can retreat to e8, defending the bishop.
notes.teaches: When your opponent overextends, use your pieces to target the weaknesses they create. A knight on f5 can be very strong, especially if it can reach d4.
notes.plans: Black will aim to play e6 or b5 to break open the center. The knight on f5 is well-placed and can later go to d4.

notes.explains: White plays f4, further weakening the kingside. Black can now strike in the center with e6, challenging the d5 pawn. White's king is exposed.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, opening the center is often the best way to launch an attack. Don't be afraid to sacrifice material to open lines.
notes.plans: Black plays e6, threatening to capture on d5. After the center opens, Black's pieces will have great activity against White's king.

notes.explains: Black plays e6, directly challenging White's center. White's bishop on e2 is passive. Black is ready to open the e-file and expose White's king.
notes.teaches: In positions with a space advantage, the side with less space should seek to trade pawns to free their pieces. Opening the center is a common method.
notes.plans: Black will capture on d5, then bring the bishop to e6 and rook to e8, putting pressure on White's king. The knight on f5 can jump to d4.

notes.explains: White recaptures with the bishop on f3, but Black can now play exd5, opening the e-file. Black's pieces are well-placed for an attack.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development and the opponent's king is exposed, opening lines is often decisive. Look for concrete tactics.
notes.plans: Black can play exd5, then Re8+ followed by Be6, developing with tempo. The bishop on d5 will be unstable, and White's king will be under fire.

notes.explains: Black plays Re8+ and Be6, developing the bishop and attacking the d5 pawn. White's king is on f2, exposed. Black has a strong initiative.
notes.teaches: When attacking, use checks and threats to bring your pieces into the game with tempo. Every move should increase the pressure.
notes.plans: Black will continue to pressure d5, possibly with b6 and Bb7, or directly capture on d5. The goal is to open lines against the white king.

notes.explains: White plays b3, but Black can now play Bb7, fianchettoing the other bishop and putting pressure on the d5 pawn. Black's pieces are very active.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, complete your development even if it means ignoring material. The extra piece will be decisive.
notes.plans: Black can play Bb7, then consider capturing on d5 or playing a move like Rc8 to increase pressure. The d5 pawn is a target.

notes.explains: Black plays Bb7, completing development. Now Black is ready to capture on d5 or play Rc8. White's position is precarious.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development and the opponent's king is exposed, it's often worth sacrificing a pawn to maintain the initiative.
notes.plans: Black can capture on d5 with the bishop or knight, or play Rc8 to pressure the knight on c3 (if it were there). The immediate threat is to win the d5 pawn.

notes.explains: White captures on b7, but this allows Black to recapture with the rook, activating it. Black's pieces are now very active.
notes.teaches: When the opponent captures a piece, consider recapturing in a way that improves your piece's activity. Here, Rxb7 brings the rook into the game.
notes.plans: Black can play Rxb7, then continue the attack with moves like Rc8 or Qe7. White's king is still exposed.

notes.explains: Black recaptures with the rook, which is now active on the b-file. Black is ready to double rooks or play Qe7. White's king is still vulnerable.
notes.teaches: In an attack, every piece should be involved. Activating the rook on an open file is a key part of building the attack.
notes.plans: Black can play Rc8, doubling rooks on the c-file, or Qe7, threatening to infiltrate. The knight on f5 can go to d4.

notes.explains: White plays Qd2, but Black can now play Ba6, threatening to win the exchange with Rc4. This is a tactical idea that exploits White's weak back rank.
notes.teaches: Look for tactics that combine threats to multiple pieces. Here, Ba6 attacks the rook on f1 and prepares Rc4, which attacks the queen and the knight.
notes.plans: Black plays Ba6, then Rc4, forcing White to deal with multiple threats. If White defends, Black can win material or deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: Black plays Rc4, attacking the queen and threatening to win the exchange. White's position is collapsing. Black's pieces are perfectly coordinated.
notes.teaches: When attacking, coordinate your pieces to create multiple threats. A rook on the fourth rank can be very powerful, especially when combined with a bishop.
notes.plans: Black will capture on c4 or force White to give up material. The attack is decisive.

notes.explains: White plays Qa3, but this allows Black to sacrifice the exchange on c4 with a decisive attack. Black's pieces are swarming around White's king.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, sacrificing material to open lines is often the fastest way to checkmate. Don't hesitate to give up material for the attack.
notes.plans: Black can play Rxc4, then follow up with checks and threats. The knight on f5 and the queen will deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: Black sacrifices the exchange with Rxc4. White cannot capture because of Qe7+ and mate threats. Black's attack is overwhelming.
notes.teaches: In a king attack, sometimes you must sacrifice material to remove defenders or open lines. The resulting position is often winning.
notes.plans: After Rxc4, Black will play Qe7+ or other checks, driving the king to a mating net. The knight on f5 controls key squares.

notes.explains: Black wins back the exchange and remains with a strong attack. White's king is still exposed, and Black's pieces are active.
notes.teaches: When attacking, keep the pressure on. Even if you win material, continue to pursue the king if it remains vulnerable.
notes.plans: Black can continue with moves like Rc8 or Nd4, increasing the pressure. The queen and knight are well-placed for a mating attack.

notes.explains: White plays Rh3, a blunder. Black can now play Qc2+ and win the rook. The game is effectively over.
notes.teaches: In a losing position, players often make mistakes. Stay alert and punish any inaccuracies.
notes.plans: Black plays Qc2+, forcing the king to move, then captures the rook on h3. The rest is technique.

notes.explains: Black wins the rook and is now up a rook. The game is easily winning. Black's king is safe, and White has no counterplay.
notes.teaches: Once you have a decisive material advantage, simplify the position and avoid unnecessary risks. Use your extra material to win.
notes.plans: Black will consolidate, activate the king, and promote a pawn. The win is straightforward.

notes.explains: White castles and plays Re1, completing development and threatening to force the queen away. Black's king is stuck in the center, and Black's queenside pieces are undeveloped.
notes.teaches: In positions with a lead in development and an exposed king, simple improving moves like castling and rook to an open file are often the most effective. Avoid speculative attacks until all pieces are coordinated.
notes.plans: White will continue with Re1, aiming to force the queen off e4. Once the queen moves, White can play Nf5+ or open the center with pawn breaks.

notes.explains: White plays Ne6+, forking the rook on d8. Black's king is exposed, and White's pieces are perfectly coordinated. The attack is decisive.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is trapped in the center and their pieces are undeveloped, a simple fork can end the game. Always look for tactical blows that exploit the opponent's lack of coordination.
notes.plans: After Ne6+, Black loses the rook or gets mated. White's attack continues with overwhelming force.

notes.explains: Black gives up the queen to avoid immediate mate, but White is up a queen for a rook and continues the attack. White now plays f4 to open lines.
notes.teaches: Even when materially ahead, continue to attack the exposed king. Use pawn breaks to open files and bring more pieces into the attack.
notes.plans: White plays f4, opening the e-file and f-file. The king has no safe haven, and White will deliver mate with queen checks.

notes.explains: White plays f4, using the pawn to open lines against the exposed king. The queen on e6 pins the e5 pawn, and White will capture on e5 to open both the e-file and f-file.
notes.teaches: When attacking a exposed king, pawn breaks are essential to open lines for your heavy pieces. Use pins to ensure the opponent cannot defend effectively.
notes.plans: White plays fxe5, opening the e-file and f-file. The king will be chased with queen checks leading to mate.

notes.explains: White captures on e5, opening both the e-file and f-file. Black's king is completely exposed, and White's queen and rook deliver mate.
notes.teaches: Once files are opened against an exposed king, the attack is often unstoppable. Use your queen and rook to deliver checks and force mate.
notes.plans: White plays Qf7+ followed by Qg7#. Black's king has no escape squares.

notes.explains: Black plays e5, creating a hole on d5, but this is acceptable because the d5-square can be defended by pieces. White's d4 leads to mass trades, transposing into a Scotch-like position without the c-pawns, which slightly favors White due to the weak d6-square.
notes.teaches: In Sicilian structures, a hole on d5 is not fatal if you can cover it with pieces; the absence of c-pawns can make d6 tender.
notes.plans: Black should develop naturally, aiming to challenge White's center and exploit the open lines.

notes.explains: Black plays Bb4, pinning the knight on c3 and pressuring e4, similar to a Four Knights Scotch. White cannot play Bd3 immediately because the knight on d4 would hang.
notes.teaches: In open positions, pins are powerful; always check if the opponent's pieces are undefended before committing to a move.
notes.plans: Black aims to maintain the pin and increase pressure on e4, possibly forcing White to weaken his position.

notes.explains: White plays Bg5, a dubious move because the bishop is undefended and White fails to address the pin on the knight. Black can exploit this with either h6 (chasing the bishop) or Qa5 (double attack).
notes.teaches: Indirect defensive moves like Bg5 are risky; if a piece is undefended, the opponent can often create a double attack or force a favorable trade.
notes.plans: Black should play h6, forcing the bishop to retreat or be captured, gaining the bishop pair and initiative.

notes.explains: Black has the bishop pair and a lead in development. White's king is stuck in the center. Black's rook on e8 pressures e4, and the pin on the knight is still active. White's Rc2 is slow; Black can now consider d5 to open the center.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is uncastled, opening the center with a pawn sacrifice can be powerful even without concrete calculation, as activity often compensates for the material.
notes.plans: Black should play d5, sacrificing a pawn to activate pieces and exploit White's king safety.

notes.explains: Black plays d5, sacrificing a pawn. White defends e4 with Bd3, but the pin on the e-file makes it hard to hold. Black can now play Bf5, threatening to win the pawn or force f3, which prevents White from castling.
notes.teaches: A pawn sacrifice in the middlegame is often a good risk if it gives you piece activity and keeps the opponent's king in the center. The threshold for risk is lower for a pawn than for a piece.
notes.plans: Black plays Bf5, aiming to force f3, then follow up with Rad8 to increase pressure on the pinned queen and the weak f2-pawn.

notes.explains: White castles, but Black wins a pawn and has a material advantage. Black's rook on d8 pins the queen, and the bishop on b6 controls dark squares. The game simplifies to a winning endgame.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, simplify by trading pieces while keeping pressure. Use pins and x-rays to target the opponent's queen, not just the king.
notes.plans: Black should trade rooks and then go after White's weak pawns, starting with a3. Combining piece activity with pawn grabbing is a reliable winning method.

notes.explains: Black simplifies further, trading rooks and bishops. White has a passed c-pawn, but Black's queen and knight easily stop it. Black can win by targeting White's king or by promoting his own pawns.
notes.teaches: In queen endgames, a passed pawn can be dangerous, but if you have a minor piece, you can often sacrifice the exchange to stop it. Look for tactics like Qf2 to deflect the rook and create mating threats.
notes.plans: Black should play Qf2, threatening mate and forcing White to give up the rook. If White tries g3, Black has Rg3 or Rd8 to maintain the attack.

notes.explains: After e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5, the Rossolimo is a positional alternative to the Open Sicilian. Black can choose between …g6 (for Accelerated Dragon players) or …e6 (for Taimanov/Paulsen players).
notes.teaches: Choose your response to the Rossolimo based on your main Sicilian repertoire. The move g6 is consistent for Accelerated Dragon players.
notes.plans: Black aims to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop and later clamp down on the d4 square with ...e5.

notes.explains: After …g6 Bxc6, Black should recapture with the d-pawn (…dxc6) rather than the bishop. This opens the diagonal for the light-squared bishop and gives the queen access to the d-file, increasing central control.
notes.teaches: Capture away from the center when it opens lines for your pieces and improves central influence.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to g7, then aim for ...e5 to clamp down on d4.

notes.explains: After ...dxc6, ...Bg7, and ...Nf6, White often plays h3 to prevent ...Bg4. Black can still play ...Bg4 anyway, trading the bishop for the knight to reduce White's control and then drop the knight back to d7.
notes.teaches: Trading a bishop for a knight can be a positional decision to relieve pressure and prepare a central pawn push.
notes.plans: Play ...Bg4, ...Bxf3, then ...Nd7, followed by ...e5 to solidify the center.

notes.explains: The knight on d7 is flexible: it can go to f8, then e6, and eventually d4, targeting the outpost. Overprotecting the e5 pawn with ...Re8 frees the knight to maneuver.
notes.teaches: Overprotection (Nimzowitsch) allows a piece to leave its defensive duty because the pawn is already sufficiently guarded.
notes.plans: Maneuver the knight from d7 to f8, then e6, and finally d4, using the rook on e8 to cover e5.

notes.explains: Bc4 is a common beginner move against the Sicilian, but e6 blunts the bishop's diagonal and prepares d5 with tempo.
notes.teaches: Against Bc4 in the Sicilian, e6 is a principled response that immediately challenges the bishop's placement.
notes.plans: Follow up with d5 to gain space and tempo, or develop normally with Nf6 and Be7.

notes.explains: After c3 (preparing d4), d5 strikes in the center with tempo, forcing an exchange that opens the position favorably for Black.
notes.teaches: When White plays c3 in the Sicilian, d5 is a strong central break that exploits the bishop's awkward position.
notes.plans: After exd5 exd5, develop naturally: Nf6, Be7, O-O, and later consider c4 or other breaks.

notes.explains: With the bishop on b3, Black should develop the knight to f6 (not e7, which blocks the dark-squared bishop).
notes.teaches: Develop knights before bishops in most positions, and avoid blocking your own pieces.
notes.plans: Play Nf6, then Be7 or Bd6, O-O, and later develop the light-squared bishop to g4 or f5.

notes.explains: c4 is a weakening move that creates a backward d2-pawn. Black can take on c4 or push d4; taking on c4 leaves White with a structural weakness.
notes.teaches: When your opponent weakens their pawn structure, consider capturing to leave them with a long-term liability.
notes.plans: After dxc4 Bxc4, develop Bd6 (exploiting that d4 is not playable due to Bxh2+), then O-O and pressure d2.

notes.explains: Bd6 is active and prevents d4 because of the tactical motif Bxh2+ winning the queen after Kxh2 Ng4+.
notes.teaches: Place bishops on active squares when the opponent cannot challenge them due to tactical threats.
notes.plans: O-O, then develop the light-squared bishop to g4, aiming for Nd4 and Bxf3 to ruin White's kingside pawns.

notes.explains: h6 prevents Bg5, which could pin the knight. This prophylactic move is useful when the opponent has no immediate threats.
notes.teaches: Prophylaxis: prevent your opponent's best moves even if they seem harmless; it limits their options.
notes.plans: After h6, develop Bg4, pinning the knight and threatening Nd4 followed by Bxf3.

notes.explains: Bg4 pins the knight. White cannot easily break the pin because Be2 is unavailable (pawn on d3 blocks). The threat is Nd4, forcing Bxf3 and ruining White's kingside pawns.
notes.teaches: A pin is powerful when the opponent cannot unravel it; combine it with threats like Nd4 to increase pressure.
notes.plans: Play Nd4, threatening Bxf3. After gxf3, Black's dark-squared bishop targets h2, and the queen can join via h4 or h3.

notes.explains: Nd4 threatens Bxf3. White's queen on b3 does not defend f3 adequately; after Bxf3 gxf3, Black's attack is overwhelming.
notes.teaches: In positions with a pinned knight, a knight jump to a central square can force a favorable exchange that destroys the opponent's pawn cover.
notes.plans: After Bxf3 gxf3, bring the queen to h4 or h3, and use the dark-squared bishop to target h2.

notes.explains: White blunders with Bxf7+, allowing a forced sequence that wins material and exposes the king. Black's attack is decisive.
notes.teaches: When attacking, look for forcing sequences that remove defenders and expose the enemy king.
notes.plans: After Bxh2+, Kxh2 Qh4+ and mate follows.

notes.explains: If White retreats the queen to d1, Black should avoid Qd7? (allows Kg2) and instead play Nh5, threatening Qh4. After g4, Qh4! is strong because the bishop cannot take (knight on h5 controls f4).
notes.teaches: In attack, bring the queen to the kingside via h4 or h3. Use knight maneuvers to control key squares like f4.
notes.plans: After Nh5 g4, Qh4 threatens Nxf3+ and mate. White must play Bd5, then Black lifts the rook to g6.

notes.explains: Black's attack is unstoppable; the queen on f4 threatens mate and the knight on h5 supports further threats.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, coordinate your queen and minor pieces to create multiple mating threats.
notes.plans: Continue with Rfe8 or Nxf4, maintaining pressure.

notes.explains: Instead of d5, Nf6 is also playable. White's best is d4, but after cxd4 cxd4, Black can play d5 with tempo, or allow the center fork trick.
notes.teaches: There are multiple good moves; choose based on your style. Nf6 leads to more tactical play.
notes.plans: After d4 cxd4 cxd4 d5, Black equalizes. Alternatively, if White plays e5, Ng4 and later d6.

notes.explains: Re1 defends e4 but allows the center fork trick: …Nxe4? Re1? Actually, the trick is …d5! exd5 Nxd5? No, the correct trick is …Nxe4! Re1 d5! forking bishop and knight.
notes.teaches: The center fork trick (Nxe4 followed by d5) is a common tactical motif when a bishop is on c4.
notes.plans: After …d5, Black wins a pawn or gets the bishop pair.

notes.explains: d3 avoids the center fork trick but allows d5, transposing to similar positions.
notes.teaches: If White avoids the trick, Black can still play d5 and develop normally.
notes.plans: After …d5, trade on d5 and develop with Be7, O-O, etc.

notes.explains: Nc3 defends e4 but allows the center fork trick in an improved form: …Nxe4? Nxe4 d5, and Black wins a pawn.
notes.teaches: When a knight defends e4, the center fork trick still works if the knight can be captured.
notes.plans: After …d5, Black wins a pawn or gets a strong initiative.

notes.explains: e5 forces Ng4, then Black plays d6 to break the center.
notes.teaches: When pushed by e5, counter in the center with d6 to undermine the pawn chain.
notes.plans: After …Ng4 Re1 d6, Black gets good piece play.

notes.explains: d4 is principled. After cxd4 cxd4, Black can play d5 or Nxe4. The trick is …Nxe4? d5!? Actually, …d5 is solid.
notes.teaches: In the Sicilian, d4 is the main break; Black must be ready to counter.
notes.plans: After …cxd4 cxd4 d5, Black equalizes. If …Nxe4, White can play d5! with complications.

notes.explains: A tactical line where Black wins a pawn but White gets compensation. Black should be careful.
notes.teaches: Tactical lines require precise calculation; sometimes it's better to avoid complications.
notes.plans: Black is a pawn up but White has development; play solidly.

notes.explains: The Fantasy Variation (f3) is recommended because it is less studied than main lines and leads to sharp tactical positions where black cannot improvise.
notes.teaches: Choose openings that are less theoretical and force opponents to think early.
notes.plans: After …dxe4 fxe4 e5, white should develop with Nf3, meeting ...Bg4 with Bc4 or c3.

notes.explains: Bc4 is more ambitious than c3; it forces black to know precise theory to avoid traps.
notes.teaches: In sharp openings, prioritize active piece development over solidifying the center.
notes.plans: After …Nd7 O-O Ngf6 c3, white solidifies the center and prepares to attack on the f-file.

notes.explains: Black's setup with ...Qe7 prepares queenside castling and threatens ...h5-h4, leading to opposite-side attacks.
notes.teaches: Recognize when the opponent is preparing opposite-side castling and plan your own attack accordingly.
notes.plans: White should complete development with Nbd2, then consider Qa4 or Qb3 to pressure the queenside.

notes.explains: Qa4 provokes ...Kb8, after which the queen drops back to b3 with an x-ray on the b-pawn. This is a practical way to create problems for a well-prepared opponent.
notes.teaches: Use provocative moves to force the opponent out of preparation; even if not objectively best, they create practical difficulties.
notes.plans: After …Kb8 Qb3, white threatens Ba6 and Nc4, pressuring the queenside and the e5 pawn.

notes.explains: Black's ...Nh5 aims to eliminate the dark-squared bishop to relieve pressure on e5. White should not panic with Bxf7; instead, stick to the queenside plan.
notes.teaches: When the opponent makes a threat, evaluate if it can be ignored or met with a stronger counter-threat.
notes.plans: White should play Ba6, threatening to force ...b6 and then jump the knight to c4, creating serious pressure on the queenside.

notes.explains: After …Nb6, white must calculate concretely. The bishop on a6 is hanging, so white needs a tempo-gaining move. Nxe5 is strong because if black recaptures, Nc6 forks the king and queen.
notes.teaches: In tactical positions, look for forcing moves that exploit the opponent's loss of control over key squares.
notes.plans: Play Nxe5, threatening Nc6+; if black avoids the fork, white wins a pawn and maintains the attack.

notes.explains: Black's ...Be6 is a strong defensive move that white underestimated. It pins the knight and threatens to win material. White must now cut losses and find the best way to give up a piece for maximum compensation.
notes.teaches: When you have miscalculated, accept the loss and look for the most graceful way to minimize damage—often by sacrificing a piece for pawns and long-term pressure.
notes.plans: Play Nxc6+ to force bxc6, then Bxd6+; white gets two pawns and continued pressure against the black king.

notes.explains: White has two pawns for the piece and practical attacking chances. The queen retreats to c2, a flexible square that keeps rooks coordinated and avoids immediate threats.
notes.teaches: When down material, give your opponent as many decisions as possible; open-ended moves can be more effective than forcing lines.
notes.plans: Start pushing the a-pawn (a4-a5) to drive away the knight on b6 and open lines against the black king.

notes.explains: White plays b4 to gain space on the queenside and prevent ...c5. This also gives black more rope to make mistakes.
notes.teaches: When attacking, use pawns to restrict the opponent's options and create targets.
notes.plans: Follow up with a5 to chase the knight away, then consider Bxc8 or Nc4 to increase pressure.

notes.explains: Nc4 brings the knight into the attack and threatens tactical ideas. Black must decide where to place the queen.
notes.teaches: Every move should pose a new problem for the opponent, especially when they are short on time.
notes.plans: After black's queen move, play Bxc8 to eliminate the bishop and continue the queenside assault.

notes.explains: White plays g3 to kick the knight from f4 and then capture the f7 pawn. This weakens the king slightly but with reduced material, it's not a problem.
notes.teaches: When down material, look for ways to win back pawns; a minor piece is only three points.
notes.plans: After ...Nh5, play Rxf7, winning a pawn and creating a passed e-pawn. Then use the rook on the seventh rank to generate tactical threats.

notes.explains: After Rxf7, white threatens Nb6+ forking king and queen. The combination of the rook on the seventh rank and the x-ray on the a-file creates a winning tactic.
notes.teaches: Look for tactical motifs like forks, discovered checks, and x-rays when you have a rook on the seventh rank.
notes.plans: Play Nb6+; if ...Nxb6, axb6 wins the queen. If ...Kb8, then Rxf8+ and axb6 is winning.

notes.explains: White's attack culminates in Qa4, threatening mate on a7. Black's king is exposed and white's pieces coordinate perfectly.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, use your queen and rook together to create mating threats; don't be afraid to sacrifice material for a decisive attack.
notes.plans: After ...Kb8, play Qa6 followed by Qb7#. If black tries to block, simply capture the blocking piece.

notes.explains: Black fianchettoed against the Grand Prix Attack, then played d6 and e6 to solidify the center. White's d4 break opened the position; Black responded with cxd4 and developed the knight to e7, a typical Botvinnik-style setup. The bishop on c4 was later retreated to b3 to prevent d5 breaks.
notes.teaches: In the Grand Prix Attack, Black's setup with ...d6 and ...e6 is solid, but combining ...g6 and ...e6 can weaken d6 if White can occupy it. Here, Black controls d6, so the combination is safe.
notes.plans: Black aims to complete development with ...b6 and ...Bb7, then challenge White's center with ...d5 or ...e5 breaks.

notes.explains: After White's knight sacrifice on d6, Black played ...f4 to block the kingside and buy time to coordinate pieces. This move hits the bishop on e3 and creates a defensive barrier, making it harder for White to infiltrate.
notes.teaches: When under attack, a pawn advance like ...f4 can serve both offensive (hitting a piece) and defensive (blocking lines) purposes, gaining a tempo to reorganize.
notes.plans: Black will follow up with ...Qc7 and ...Rfd8 to target the knight on d6, then eventually bring the knight to g6 to solidify the e5 pawn.

notes.explains: In the endgame, Black is up a piece but must be careful due to White's active rook and potential mating threats. After ...b4, Black missed a drawing resource: White could play Bxa8, leading to a line where ...bxc3, Bf1, c2, Ke2, Na3, Kd1, Nc4, a4! forces a draw by repetition because the knight cannot escape via b5.
notes.teaches: In endgames with a material advantage, prophylaxis is key. Look for ways to neutralize opponent's counterplay before executing your own plan. Here, ...Rc4 would have been safer than ...Rxe4, avoiding complications.
notes.plans: Black should consolidate by bringing the bishop back to g7 and doubling rooks, then slowly convert the extra piece.

notes.explains: Black missed the winning continuation after ...b4. Instead of Bxa8, White played Rxf7, allowing Black to win with Nf3+! The knight fork wins the game because after gxf3, Rxe7, Rxa8, Bxc3, Black is up a full rook.
notes.teaches: Always look for tactical resources like knight forks, especially when the opponent's king is exposed. A fresh perspective can reveal winning moves that are easy to overlook.
notes.plans: After Nf3+, Black wins material and should convert by activating the remaining pieces.

notes.explains: Black chooses a Grünfeld-like setup with g6, but White's pawn is on e4 rather than c4, leading to a fundamentally different game.
notes.teaches: The Jobava London often arises after d4 Nc3, and if Black plays d5, White can push e4 to reach this sharp, tactical line.
notes.plans: White aims to launch a kingside attack with h4-h5, often sacrificing the exchange on h5 to open lines.

notes.explains: White immediately pushes the h-pawn, a key idea in this line. If Black allows h5, White can sacrifice the exchange on h5 for a powerful attack.
notes.teaches: Early h-pawn pushes can be legitimate, especially when Black has fianchettoed. The idea is to open the h-file and create attacking chances.
notes.plans: White wants to play h5, and if Black takes, recapture with the rook, then follow up with Qh5, threatening d5 and other weaknesses.

notes.explains: Black stops h5 with h5, freezing the kingside structure. White continues development with Nf3, preparing to castle queenside and later play g4.
notes.teaches: When the h-pawn is blocked, White can still prepare g4 to break open the kingside. The attack often involves opposite-side castling.
notes.plans: White castles queenside, then plays g4 to force open the h-file, using the queen and rooks to deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: Black plays c5, a typical queenside counter. White cannot play c3 to support d4, but the knight on c3 eyes d5. White can capture on c5 or play Ne5.
notes.teaches: In the Jobava London, c5 is a common response. White must decide whether to take on c5 or maintain the pawn on d4. The knight on c3 provides pressure on d5.
notes.plans: White can consider dxc5, but the recommended move is Ne5, preparing f3 and g4. Taking on c5 can lead to complications if Black knows the theory.

notes.explains: White played dxc5, but this is a mistake. Black responds with Nbd7, threatening to recapture on c5 and also eyeing d5. White cannot take on d5 due to tactics.
notes.teaches: Taking on c5 can be dangerous if Black knows the refutation. The move Nbd7 is strong because it prepares to recapture and keeps d5 defended indirectly.
notes.plans: White must now play Ne5 to avoid losing material. The position is tricky, and White should have played Ne5 earlier instead of dxc5.

notes.explains: White plays Ne5 and f3, preparing g4 and controlling e4. The knight on e5 is well-placed, and f3 prevents Black's knights from jumping to e4.
notes.teaches: f3 serves two purposes: it prepares the g4 break and restricts Black's knights. Controlling e4 is crucial to maintain the attack.
notes.plans: White will castle queenside and then play g4 to open the kingside. The queen on d2 can later move to h2 to threaten checkmate.

notes.explains: Black develops the bishop to f5, eyeing the queenside. White considers g4 but decides it's premature. Instead, White castles queenside to safety.
notes.teaches: When opposite-side castling, it's important to secure your king before launching the attack. g4 can be delayed if it's not fully prepared.
notes.plans: White castles queenside (O-O-O), then prepares g4. The immediate threat is Nxd5, but White must be careful about tactics on the queenside.

notes.explains: Black retreats the bishop to e6, a passive move that loses time. This gives White the opportunity to play g4 now that the king is safe.
notes.teaches: In opposite-side castling positions, every tempo counts. Black's passive move allows White to seize the initiative with the g4 break.
notes.plans: White plays g4 to open the kingside. The queen on d2 can go to h2, threatening checkmate on h7. Black's bishop on e6 is misplaced.

notes.explains: White plays g4, the thematic break. Black can take on g4, but White then recaptures with the f-pawn, opening the f-file and preparing h5.
notes.teaches: The g4 break is a classic attacking idea in fianchetto positions. It opens lines for the rooks and queen, often leading to a devastating attack.
notes.plans: If Black takes on g4, White recaptures with f3xg4, then pushes h5. The queen can go to h2, and the rooks join the attack via the h-file.

notes.explains: Black plays Qa5, pressuring a2 and the queenside. White responds with Kb1, a standard defensive move that also sets up a tactical threat.
notes.teaches: When opposite-side castling, it's crucial to defend your king. Kb1 is a typical move that also prepares potential tactics like Nxd5.
notes.plans: White threatens Nxd5, which would win material due to the discovered attack on the queen. Black must be careful not to fall for this tactic.

notes.explains: Black plays Rfc8, bringing the rook to the c-file. White now has the tactical opportunity Nxd5, which wins material due to the queen on a5.
notes.teaches: When the queen is on a5 and the rook on c8, Nxd5 can be a powerful tactic. Black cannot recapture because the queen would be lost.
notes.plans: White plays Nxd5. If Black captures the queen, White recaptures with the rook and then plays Nxe7+, winning a pawn. The knight may be trapped, but White can try to extricate it.

notes.explains: White executes the tactic: Nxd5, forcing queen trade, then Nxe7+ winning a pawn. Black's king moves to h8, and White recaptures on d5, emerging with two extra pawns.
notes.teaches: This sequence illustrates a classic desperado tactic: when a piece is attacked, you can often sacrifice it for material gain if you have intermediate checks.
notes.plans: White is up two pawns but the knight on e7 is trapped. White must find a way to save the knight, possibly by playing g5 to open lines or by sacrificing it for more pawns.

notes.explains: Black plays Rxc2, attacking the bishop on f4 and threatening back-rank mate. White must respond carefully to avoid losing the knight on e7.
notes.teaches: After a sequence of exchanges, it's easy to overlook threats like back-rank mate. Always update your perception of the board after each exchange.
notes.plans: White can play Rd4, a collinear move that defends the rook and prepares to extricate the knight. Alternatively, White can play Nxg6, sacrificing the knight for pawns.

notes.explains: White plays Rd4, a collinear move that places the rook on a defended square (by the pawn on e4) while keeping the file open. This defends against back-rank threats and prepares to save the knight.
notes.teaches: A collinear move is when you move a piece onto the same line as two opposing pieces, but not capturing. It can be a powerful defensive or tactical idea.
notes.plans: White threatens Nxg6, winning more pawns. Black must respond, and White can then extricate the knight via d5 or g8.

notes.explains: Black captures on g4. White now has the opportunity to play h5, opening the h-file and threatening the knight on h5. The knight on e7 is also well-placed to support the attack.
notes.teaches: In opposite-side castling positions, even after queens are traded, the h-file can still be a decisive attacking avenue. The knight on e7 can aid in checkmate patterns.
notes.plans: White plays h5, threatening to open the h-file. If Black captures on h5, White recaptures with the pawn, opening lines. The knight on e7 prevents the black king from escaping.

notes.explains: Black captures on h5. White now plays fxg4, opening the f-file and threatening the knight on h5. The knight on e7 is pinned, and White can win material.
notes.teaches: When the h-file is opened, the rook on h1 becomes a powerful attacker. The pinned knight on h5 is vulnerable, and White can exploit it.
notes.plans: White plays fxg4, threatening to capture the knight on h5. Black's best try is to play Bxg4, but then White has Rxd8+ and other tactics.

notes.explains: Black plays Bxg4, trying to gain material. White can now play Rxd8+ and then Nxg6+, winning the rook on f8 and the bishop on g4.
notes.teaches: When the opponent tries to counterattack, look for intermediate checks and captures that win material. Avoid tunnel vision and consider all tactical possibilities.
notes.plans: White plays Rxd8+ first, then Nxg6+ forking king and rook. After the king moves, White captures the rook on f8, winning a huge amount of material.

notes.explains: White executes the winning sequence: Rxd8+, Nxg6+, and Nxf8, emerging with a rook and multiple pawns for two pieces. The knight on e7 is safe and can be evacuated.
notes.teaches: This sequence demonstrates how to convert a material advantage by forcing exchanges and simplifying. The knight on e7 can later be brought to d5 or f4.
notes.plans: White is up a rook and several pawns. The knight on e7 can be evacuated via d5 or g8. White should consolidate and then push for checkmate or further material gain.

notes.explains: White plays Nd5, evacuating the knight to a safe square. The knight is well-placed in the center, and White can now bring the bishop into play.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, centralize your pieces. The knight on d5 is strong and can later move to f4 or e3 to support the attack.
notes.plans: White will bring the bishop to d3 or e2, then use the rook to target Black's weak pawns. The knight can go to f4 to pressure h5.

notes.explains: White plays Nf4, targeting the pawn on h5 and creating a strong outpost. The knight is defended by the pawn on g2 and cannot be easily dislodged.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, knights on outposts can be very powerful. Nf4 attacks h5 and supports a future advance of the kingside pawns.
notes.plans: White will play Bg2 or Bd3, then push the kingside pawns. Black's pawn on h5 is weak and can be captured.

notes.explains: Black plays Rc5, attacking the pawn on g5. White can defend with Bg2 or simply advance the pawn. The position is winning for White.
notes.teaches: When up material, it's often best to simplify. White can trade rooks or bishops to reduce Black's counterplay.
notes.plans: White can play Bg2, then Rg3 or Rh3. Alternatively, White can play g6 to open lines. The key is to avoid unnecessary complications.

notes.explains: White plays Bd3, activating the bishop and threatening to trade on f5. This simplifies the position and removes Black's active bishop.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, trade pieces to reduce counterplay. Bd3 forces Black to either trade or retreat, both of which favor White.
notes.plans: After Bd3, White can play Rg3 or Rh3. The knight on f4 is well-placed, and White can push the kingside pawns.
