notes.explains: White pushes g6, opening lines and threatening to create a passed pawn. Black's rook is passive, and White's knight and rook are active.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, creating passed pawns is a key winning method. g6 opens the f-file and supports the advance of the h-pawn.
notes.plans: White will play Rh3 or Rg3, then push the h-pawn. Black's king is cut off, and White's pieces dominate.

notes.explains: White plays Nd5, forking the rook and pawn on e7. Black must give up material. The knight is a powerful piece in this endgame.
notes.teaches: Knights are often stronger than rooks in closed positions. Nd5 creates a double threat that wins material.
notes.plans: After Nd5, Black will lose the pawn on e7 or the rook. White will then have a decisive material advantage.

notes.explains: White sacrifices two pawns for a big lead in development and central control, aiming for a quick attack.
notes.teaches: In gambits, development and initiative often outweigh material; black must neutralize White's lead before cashing in the extra pawns.
notes.plans: Black should accept the gambit pawns but then carefully coordinate pieces to blunt White's attack and consolidate the material advantage.

notes.explains: White offers the first pawn with c3. Black can accept or decline; declining with d5 is a practical alternative that leads to equal but comfortable positions.
notes.teaches: Declining a gambit with a central counterstrike can take the fun out of White's attack and lead to a solid position.
notes.plans: After …d5, White's best is exd5; black recaptures with the queen, then develops with Nc6 and Bb4+, aiming for an endgame where White's isolated d-pawn is a weakness.

notes.explains: White recaptures with the knight, offering only one pawn. Black must avoid Nf6 due to e5; instead develop the dark-squared bishop to c5 and solidify with d6.
notes.teaches: In gambit lines, delaying knight development can prevent tactical shots like e5. Prioritize bishop development and pawn solidity.
notes.plans: Play Bc5, d6, then Nf6 after White's e5 is neutralized. If White plays Qb3, counter with Qh4 attacking f2. After g3, drop back to f6, then e7 to stop Nd5 and prepare Nf6.

notes.explains: White offers a second pawn with Bc4. Black should accept with Nf6, not the old D5 line which gives White easy equality. After e5, check with Bb4.
notes.teaches: Accepting the second pawn is principled; the old D5 sacrifice is outdated. The check on b4 forces White to defend awkwardly.
notes.plans: Play Nf6, then after e5, Bb4+. Against most White replies (Nc3, Nd2, Kf1), counter with d5. Against the best reply Bc3, play Qe7 pinning the e-pawn and preparing to redeploy the knight via g8-h6.

notes.explains: White blocks the check with Nc3, the most common move, but it loses on the spot. Black plays d5, counterattacking the center.
notes.teaches: When White's pieces are hanging, a central pawn break can exploit the lack of coordination. Here d5 attacks both the bishop and knight.
notes.plans: After …d5, if exf6, recapture with the queen (Qxf6) hitting both the knight and bishop. White cannot defend both, so Black wins at least a pawn with a winning position.

notes.explains: White moves the king. Black again plays d5, leading to an endgame where White gets a pawn on g7. Black's plan is to surround and win that pawn.
notes.teaches: In endgames, a single extra pawn is often decisive if the opponent has no counterplay. Patience and accurate technique are required.
notes.plans: After exf6, play Qxf6, then develop with Nc6, Bf5, and rook to g8. Target the g7 pawn with moves like Nd7, f6, and Bg6. White's king is exposed, giving Black additional attacking chances.

notes.explains: White blocks with the bishop, the best but rare move. Black should not play d5 here; instead play Qe7, pinning the e-pawn and guarding the bishop.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's best move is rare, it's still essential to know the correct response. Pinning a pawn can prevent a dangerous advance.
notes.plans: Play Qe7. If White takes on b4, recapture with the queen and then play Nd2-e4 with initiative. If White plays Qe2, retreat the knight to g8 and redeploy to h6, then castle and aim for d6 to trade off the e5 pawn.

notes.explains: After d4 Nf6 Nf3 d5 Bf4, White's Nc3 instead of c3 exerts pressure on d5. Black's c5 is a mistake because dxc5 leaves Black struggling to regain the pawn without falling behind in development. a3 prepares b4 to secure the c5 pawn, and after e5 Bg5, Black must waste a tempo with Be6 to prevent Bxf6 Nxd5. b4 then secures the pawn, leaving White up a pawn with no compensation.
notes.teaches: In the Jobava London, the knight on c3 changes the character of the London system, allowing aggressive pawn grabs like dxc5. The move a3 is a key prophylactic idea to support the c5 pawn and prepare b4.
notes.plans: White should continue development with Nf3 and Be2, aiming to consolidate the extra pawn and restrict Black's piece activity.

notes.explains: After Qd7, Na4 becomes effective because it threatens Nb6, forking the queen and bishop. This increases pressure on Black's position and exploits the queen's placement.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen moves to d7, a knight jump to a4 can create tactical threats (Nb6 fork). This is a common motif in the Jobava London.
notes.plans: White should aim to play Nb6, forcing Black to deal with the fork, and then continue developing while maintaining the extra pawn.

notes.explains: Black's Qe8 is a brilliant move that sets up the threat of Ne4. If White castles, Black can play Ne4, and after Bxe7 Qxe7, the knight on c3 is undefended, leading to tactical complications. White's best response is Na4, which takes the sting out of Ne4 by moving the knight away from the vulnerable square.
notes.teaches: Always consider your opponent's hidden threats. Qe8 prepares Ne4, exploiting the undefended knight on c3. Prophylactic moves like Na4 can neutralize such ideas.
notes.plans: White should play Na4, then continue development, keeping the extra pawn and avoiding the tactical trap.

notes.explains: After White castles, Black plays Ne4, leading to a sequence where White ends up with a rook and two pawns for two minor pieces. This is a typical material imbalance. The evaluation depends on piece activity: White's rook needs to become active immediately.
notes.teaches: When you have a rook for two minor pieces, prioritize rook activity. Place the rook on an open file and aim to dominate the minor pieces with long-range threats.
notes.plans: White should play Rfd1, putting the rook on the only open file, and then look to double rooks or occupy the d6 outpost. The rook on d6 can serve as an anchor point.

notes.explains: White's rook on d6 is well-placed, but Black's Qg5 is a strong move targeting g2. White prevents it with Qh5, and then both sides make useful moves: h3 creates luft, and Rf8 is a slight inaccuracy as it wastes time. Black should have played Qf6 immediately to pressure White.
notes.teaches: In rook vs. minor pieces, the side with the rook should seek to activate the rook and create luft for the king. The side with the minor pieces should aim to keep the opponent's pawns immobile and target weaknesses.
notes.plans: White should continue improving piece placement, possibly preparing c4 to break through on the queenside. Black should have played Qf6 to attack f2 and keep pressure.

notes.explains: After Qxb7, White has a rook and two pawns for two minor pieces, with a passed b-pawn. Black's queen is active, but White's king is safe. The key idea is to trade queens or rooks to reduce Black's defensive resources. A rook trade favors the side with the rook because minor pieces are poor at multitasking.
notes.teaches: In rook vs. minor piece endgames, trading rooks often benefits the side with the rook because the minor pieces struggle to defend multiple weaknesses. Similarly, trading queens can leave the minor pieces unable to stop a passed pawn.
notes.plans: White should aim to trade queens, e.g., with Qd5, and then push the b-pawn. If Black avoids the trade, White can use the rook to support the pawn's advance.

notes.explains: After e4 c5, White's Bc4 is a harmless move because Black can later play e6 to block the bishop's diagonal to f7.
notes.teaches: Developing the bishop to c4 against the Sicilian is ineffective when Black can play e6, shutting the bishop out.
notes.plans: Black should develop naturally with Nc6 and Nf6, then prepare d5 to challenge the center.

notes.explains: After e4 c5 Bc4 Nc6 Nf3 a6 a3 Nf6 Nc3 e6 Ba2 d5, Black has a comfortable position with central control.
notes.teaches: When facing sidelines, following basic principles (develop, control the center) often yields a good position.
notes.plans: Black can continue with Be7, 0-0, and later consider expanding or piece play.

notes.explains: After exd5 exd5 Nf3, Black should consider Bg4 to prevent White from playing d4. This violates the usual priority of kingside development but is active and stops d4.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a developing move that prevents the opponent's central break is more important than castling immediately.
notes.plans: If White castles, Black can play Be7 and then consider Nd4 or other central breaks.

notes.explains: After …Bg4 9.0-0 Be7 h3, Black can play Bh5, inviting g4. If White pushes g4 and g5, the king becomes exposed, and Black can sacrifice the d5 pawn for long-term compensation.
notes.teaches: Do not fear minor material sacrifices when the opponent's king becomes vulnerable. The long-term weakness of the king outweighs a pawn.
notes.plans: After Bh5 g4 Bg6, Black can play h6 to prevent g5, or castle and later use the open lines.

notes.explains: After d3 h6 12.0-0, Black should consider Queen D7 to connect rooks and prepare central play, but must be aware of the threat g5 with tempo, putting pressure on d5.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a pawn storm on the kingside, be careful about moves that allow them to gain tempo and increase pressure.
notes.plans: Black might consider Bd6 to neutralize the bishop on f4, or play Rfe8 and keep the tension.

notes.explains: After Bf4 Qd7 Rfe1, White's Knight F4 threatens the bishop on g6. Black should retreat the bishop to h7, then play b5 and c4 to shut down White's bad bishop on a2.
notes.teaches: Use pawns to restrict the opponent's bad pieces. A restricted bishop is a long-term asset.
notes.plans: After Bh7 Nf4, play b5 and c4, then continue with Rfd8 or other improving moves.

notes.explains: After Bh7 Nf4 b5 c4, Black has locked White's bishop on a2. Now Black can consider Queen C8, a retreating move that takes the sting out of Ne5 and creates an x-ray against White's queen.
notes.teaches: Retreating moves can be just as important as advancing ones. They improve the position without creating weaknesses.
notes.plans: After Qc8, Black can play Rfd8, then look for tactical opportunities like Ne4 if White's rook leaves d1.

notes.explains: After Qc8 Rd2, Black can play Ne4. If dxe4 dxe4, White's best is Nxd5, but then Black has Rxd5 followed by Rd8, exploiting the undefended rook on d1.
notes.teaches: In complex positions, always update which pieces are undefended. A seemingly quiet move like Rd2 can create tactical opportunities.
notes.plans: After Ne4, if White avoids the line, Black can continue with Nxg3 or other threats.

notes.explains: After Ne4 dxe4 dxe4, White played Nxg3 instead of the stronger Ng5. Ng5 would have opened the d4 square for a fork, but Black is still better.
notes.teaches: Retreating knight moves can be very powerful, especially when they open up key squares for forks.
notes.plans: After Nxg3, Black recaptures and continues with positional pressure.

notes.explains: After hxg3 d4, White's d4 is a mistake because it opens the diagonal for Black's bishop and gives Black the e4 square. Black can play Qb8, then Be4, dominating the center.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a bad bishop, do not open the position for it unless you have concrete compensation.
notes.plans: Black plays Qb8, Be4, then Rfe8, and eventually pushes a5-b4 to attack the queenside.

notes.explains: After Qb8 Rfe8 Be4 c3, Black's a5-b4 push breaks through on the queenside. White cannot take on b4 because of the fork threat e3.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are tied down, a pawn break on the queenside can be decisive. Always check for tactical details like pawn forks.
notes.plans: After bxa5, Black plays b4, then Ba6, winning the bishop on b1.

notes.explains: After bxa5 b4 Bb1 Ba6, Black wins the bishop. White's position collapses.
notes.teaches: Consistent pressure forces the opponent to make mistakes. The collapse often happens in one or two moves.
notes.plans: Black takes the bishop, then simplifies to a winning endgame or checkmates.

notes.explains: After winning a piece, White must avoid moves like Bb5+ that allow c6, leading to unnecessary complications. Instead, retreat the bishop to b3.
notes.teaches: When up material, avoid giving the opponent counterplay. Choose simple, solid moves that maintain your advantage.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to b3, then play d3 to eliminate the e4 pawn and open lines for the dark-squared bishop.

notes.explains: Black's c5-c4 push does nothing because c4 is defended by the bishop. White's priority is to complete development and remove the e4 pawn, which is a hindrance.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is 'hanging over' your position, removing it (e.g., with d3) can improve piece coordination and open lines.
notes.plans: Play d3, then develop the dark-squared bishop to g5 or f4, and eventually castle queenside to bring the rook to the d-file.

notes.explains: After trading bishops and queens, White's king is safe, and the knight on d5 is a powerful outpost. Castling queenside brings the rook to the open d-file.
notes.teaches: When up material, trade pieces to reduce counterplay. An outpost like d5 for the knight is a long-term asset.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to f4 (safe square), then castle queenside and double rooks on the d-file.

notes.explains: Black's c4 push opens the d4 square for the knight. White castles queenside, defending the knight with the rook and preparing to double rooks.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is pushed, look for new squares for your pieces. Doubling rooks on an open file is a standard way to increase pressure.
notes.plans: Play Rd2, then Rd1 to double rooks, then move the knight away from d4 to open the file for the rooks.

notes.explains: White doubles rooks on the d-file, then moves the knight to f5 (an ideal square). The e4 pawn is defended, and Black has no threats.
notes.teaches: When converting a material advantage, you don't need to grab every pawn. Focus on activating your pieces and simplifying.
notes.plans: After Nf5, trade bishops if possible, then trade rooks and create a passed pawn.

notes.explains: White uses the rook to win pawns and create a passed c-pawn. The rook cuts off the black king, allowing the pawn to promote.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, cutting off the enemy king with your rook is a powerful technique to promote a pawn. Always be careful not to stalemate.
notes.plans: Push the c-pawn, use the queen to drive the king to the back rank, and deliver checkmate with the rook.

notes.explains: The immediate d4 is a mistake because Black plays Qh4+ and White cannot block with g3 due to the f-pawn. White must move the king to e2, which is dangerous.
notes.teaches: Never play d4 before Nf3 in the King's Gambit, as it allows a devastating queen check.
notes.plans: Black should play d5 after Qh4+, sacrificing a pawn to develop rapidly and attack the exposed white king.

notes.explains: Black plays d5 immediately, sacrificing a pawn to open lines and develop the bishop to g4 with check. White's king is stuck on e2.
notes.teaches: When the white king is exposed, sacrifice material to accelerate development and launch an attack.
notes.plans: Black aims to castle queenside and bring the knight to d7, targeting the white king. White's king will never be safe.

notes.explains: Nc3 is a Vienna-style move that allows Qh4+ and Ke2, then Nf3 chasing the queen. Black can play d5 anyway, sacrificing a pawn for rapid development.
notes.teaches: Against Nc3, Black should still play d5, ignoring the threat to the e5 pawn. The exposed white king compensates for the material.
notes.plans: After d5, Black develops with Bg4, Bd6, and Nc6, threatening Nd4+ and targeting the white king.

notes.explains: Black ignores the threat to c7 and plays Nc6, threatening Nd4+. If White plays d4, Black castles and takes on f4, then Nf6 attacks the knight on d5.
notes.teaches: When the white king is exposed, prioritize threats against the king over material. The knight on d5 is illusory because White's king is vulnerable.
notes.plans: Black will take on f4 and f3, winning the queen or delivering checkmate. White's position collapses despite the central pawns.

notes.explains: After Nxa8, Black plays Ne5, threatening to take on f3 and then Qh5+ winning the queen. White cannot stop this plan easily.
notes.teaches: Even when a piece is trapped, look for tactical threats that exploit the opponent's king safety. The knight on a8 is irrelevant if White's king is exposed.
notes.plans: Black will take on f3, then Qh5+ and capture the queen. The knight on a8 will be trapped, leaving Black with a winning position.

notes.explains: White plays d4, but Black executes the sacrifice on f3, then Qh5+ wins the queen. The king on a dark square prevents a discovered check from saving White.
notes.teaches: Always ensure the opponent's king cannot escape via discovered checks. Here, the dark-square king is crucial for the tactic to work.
notes.plans: Black wins the queen and remains with a material advantage and a weak white king.

notes.explains: After the queen trade, Black plays g5 to prevent the bishop on c1 from evacuating the knight on a8 via c7. This prophylactic move secures the trapped knight.
notes.teaches: In endgames with a trapped piece, use pawn moves to restrict the opponent's pieces and prevent rescue attempts.
notes.plans: Black will play Nf6, targeting e4, then Kc8 and Kb8 to free the knight. The knight on a8 is not going anywhere.

notes.explains: If White plays e5, Black meets with Nh6, then exf6 Bd6, aiming to develop kingside pieces quickly so that f7 does not trap the rook. The rook goes to c8, not f8, to avoid Bg7 fork.
notes.teaches: When the opponent tries to trap a rook, develop pieces to cover escape squares. Here, Bd6 prevents Bg7 and allows Rc8.
notes.plans: Black will pick up the pawn on f7 and the knight on a8, ending with two pieces for a rook and a dominant position.

notes.explains: Against Bc4, Black does not play Qh4+ because the king can go to f1, which is safer than e2. Instead, Black develops with Nc6.
notes.teaches: Do not automatically check if it helps the opponent improve their king. Here, Qh4+ would allow White to escape to f1 with a safer position.
notes.plans: Black will play Nc6, and if d4, then Qh4+ followed by d6, pinning the knight with Bg4 and forcing a queen trade.

notes.explains: After Nf3, Black plays g5, supporting the pawn. The bishop on c4 is poorly placed, and Black will play h6 and Ne7, building a solid setup.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's bishop is on c4, the g5 push is safe because White cannot easily attack the pawn. Black's setup is solid and a pawn up.
notes.plans: Black will play Bg7, h6, Ne7, and castle, maintaining the extra pawn with no compensation for White.

notes.explains: Black plays Qd7, leaving e7 free for the knight and preparing Na5 to trade off the bishop on c4. This neutralizes White's compensation.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's bishop is a key attacking piece, aim to trade it off. Here, Na5 forces a favorable exchange.
notes.plans: After Na5, Black will trade bishops and castle, leaving White with no attack and a pawn deficit.

notes.explains: Bc4 blunders a pawn. Black can simply take on f4. If Qe2, Black plays Qe7 and White only wins back one pawn, leaving Black with a superior endgame.
notes.teaches: Always check if the opponent's move hangs a pawn. In the Schallopp, Bc4 is a common mistake that gives Black an easy advantage.
notes.plans: Black takes on f4, then plays d5 and c6, building a queenside pawn wedge. The bishop on c4 is out of play.

notes.explains: d3 is passive. Black plays d5, and if exd5, then Bxf4. The computer prefers Nc6 development, but d5 is fine.
notes.teaches: Against passive moves, strike in the center. d5 opens lines and challenges White's control.
notes.plans: Black will develop with Nc6, Bb4 or Bg4, and maintain the extra pawn.

notes.explains: Nc3 is a main line. Black plays d5, striking the center. If exd5, then Nxd5 and Black can play Qe7+ or retreat the knight to b6.
notes.teaches: Against Nc3, the central break d5 is key. It challenges White's pawn center and opens lines for Black's pieces.
notes.plans: Black will develop with Nc6, Bg4, and consider queenside castling if White's king is exposed.

notes.explains: After the queen exchange, Black plays Be7, not Bd6. The point is that Bxf4 is a trap: if White takes, Black wins the bishop with ...g5.
notes.teaches: In the Schallopp, Be7 is a precise move that sets a trap. Always look for tactical opportunities when recapturing pawns.
notes.plans: Black will develop with Nc6, and if White plays c4, the queen drops back to d6 or f6. Black aims to castle and use the d5 outpost.

notes.explains: Black sacrifices the f4 pawn to get quick development. The bishop on e6 will go to d5, a fantastic outpost, and White's center is weak.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it is worth giving back the pawn to activate your pieces and create long-term positional trumps like an outpost.
notes.plans: Black will castle queenside and target White's weak pawns. The knight on d5 is a monster.

notes.explains: If White plays Bd3, Black defends the f4 pawn with g5. White's bishop on d3 is passive, and Black maintains the extra pawn.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's bishop is not threatening, simply hold the pawn and continue development.
notes.plans: Black will play Nc6, Qc7, and castle queenside, keeping the extra pawn.

notes.explains: After e5 Nh5 d4, Black plays d6, not d5. The reason is that d5 would allow c4, undermining Black's center. With d6, Black avoids that and prepares f6.
notes.teaches: In the Schallopp, the move d6 is more flexible than d5 because it prevents White from playing c4 and undermining the center.
notes.plans: Black will play g6 or g5, then Nc6, and eventually f6 to break White's center.

notes.explains: If White plays Bc4, Black takes on e5 and forces queen trade, then Bg4+ wins the pawn on f4. Black is a pawn up with a better endgame.
notes.teaches: In the Schallopp, trading queens often favors Black because White's king is exposed and Black has the extra pawn.
notes.plans: Black will develop and enjoy a pawn-up endgame with active pieces.

notes.explains: After Qe2, Black trades queens and then plays Nc6, threatening Nd4+ and targeting the f4 pawn. White's king is exposed.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, centralize your pieces and create threats. The knight on c6 is well placed.
notes.plans: Black will take on f4 and maintain the extra pawn with active pieces.

notes.explains: Black sacrifices the knight on d4 to win the f4 pawn and expose the white king. After Bxf4, Black has two pawns and a strong attack.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a piece sacrifice is justified to destroy the opponent's pawn structure and expose the king.
notes.plans: Black will continue with ...O-O-O and ...Rd8, targeting the white king.

notes.explains: If White plays Be2 (a rare move by Shaw), Black plays Nc6 and then g6. The idea is to avoid g5 because of d5, which would be strong for White. g6 is safer.
notes.teaches: When the opponent targets the knight, use g6 to create a safe retreat and support the center. g5 can be met by d5, so g6 is more solid.
notes.plans: Black will play Bg7, O-O, and then f6 to break White's center.

notes.explains: Black plays f6 to undermine White's center. The knight on h5 is safe via g7. Black's position is solid and active.
notes.teaches: In the Schallopp, the move f6 is a key break to challenge White's pawn center. The knight can retreat to g7 or f5.
notes.plans: Black will open the center and activate the bishops, targeting White's king.

notes.explains: After a forcing sequence, Black ends up with a monster pawn chain on the kingside and active bishops. The queen on e5 is well placed.
notes.teaches: In tactical melees, keep your pieces active and create pawn chains that restrict the opponent.
notes.plans: Black will play ...Qe7 and ...Bf5, with a dominant position. White's king is exposed.

notes.explains: After queen trade, Black has a knight vs bishop endgame with a pawn chain. Black's knight is active and White's pawns are weak.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, active pieces and pawn structure matter more than material. Black's knight on f5 is a monster.
notes.plans: Black will target White's weak pawns and use the knight to create threats.

notes.explains: Black's knight goes to d6, attacking the c4 pawn and eyeing e4. White's pawns are weak and Black has a clear advantage.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, centralize your knight and target weak pawns. The knight on d6 is perfectly placed.
notes.plans: Black will win the c4 pawn and then advance the kingside pawns.

notes.explains: If White plays Bc4, Black trades queens and then plays Bg4+ and Nc6, threatening Nd4. White's king is stuck in the center.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, use checks and threats to prevent them from castling.
notes.plans: Black will take on f4 and develop with ...O-O-O, attacking the white king.

notes.explains: Black sacrifices the knight on d4 to expose the king and deliver a check with ...O-O-O+. White's king is under attack.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is in the center, use sacrifices to open lines and bring your rook into the attack.
notes.plans: Black will continue with ...Rd8 and ...Bxf4, with a winning attack.

notes.explains: After a complex sequence, Black ends up with a rook and two pawns for two pieces, but the white king is exposed and Black has a strong attack.
notes.teaches: In tactical positions, material is not the only factor. King safety and initiative matter more.
notes.plans: Black will continue the attack with ...Rd8 and ...Re8, targeting the white king.

notes.explains: Black's rooks double on the d-file, and the white king is chased to b6. Black has a decisive attack.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, double rooks on an open file to create mating threats.
notes.plans: Black will play ...R8d6 and ...Rb5+ to force checkmate or win material.

notes.explains: After a long forcing line, Black wins material and ends up with a rook and pawns against a knight. Black's pawns are strong.
notes.teaches: In complicated variations, stay calm and calculate accurately. The resulting endgame is winning for Black.
notes.plans: Black will advance the kingside pawns and use the rook to support them.

notes.explains: After e4 d5 exd5 Nf6, White cannot keep the extra pawn with c4 because Black replies …c6, leading to either a Panov–Botvinnik Attack or dxc6 Nxc6 with a strong center and a bad light-squared bishop for White.
notes.teaches: In the Scandinavian, White should not cling to the pawn; instead, seek active development with tempo.
notes.plans: Play Bb5+ to provoke a weakening move, then retreat to e2 to prevent ...Bg4.

notes.explains: Bb5+ is a developing move with tempo. Black's best reply is …Bd7, which blocks the b8-knight and cuts communication between queen and center, making the bishop poorly placed.
notes.teaches: Provoke the opponent into making a move that impairs their own development.
notes.plans: After …Bd7, retreat the bishop to e2 to prevent ...Bg4, then build the center with d4.

notes.explains: Be2 is necessary to stop ...Bg4, which would attack the queen and improve Black's bishop. Moving the bishop also prevents Black from trading it off later with ...a6 and ...Bxb5.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you must retreat a piece to a less active square to neutralize a threat and maintain your structural advantage.
notes.plans: Follow with d4, then Nf3, O-O, and c4 to challenge the knight on d5.

notes.explains: White plays Nf3 instead of c3, allowing Black to capture on d4. White then develops Bd3, ignoring the pawn deficit, to maintain the clamp on e5 and prepare kingside play.
notes.teaches: In closed structures, rapid development and piece activity can outweigh material concerns. The e5 pawn acts as a clamp, restricting Black's development.
notes.plans: White aims to complete kingside development quickly, then win back the d4 pawn with Nb1-d2-b3, while keeping the e5 pawn intact.

notes.explains: White castles and develops the knight to b3, pressuring d4 and preparing to recapture the pawn. Black's bishop on c5 retreats to b6 to avoid exchanges.
notes.teaches: The knight on b3 is ideally placed: it attacks d4, does not block the bishops, and supports a future Greek Gift sacrifice on h7.
notes.plans: White will eventually win back the d4 pawn, often after Black castles into a Greek Gift attack. If Black delays castling, White can still regain the pawn with Nb3xd4.

notes.explains: Black avoids the Greek Gift by delaying castling and playing Bd7. White can still win back the pawn with Nb3xd4, and after Nxd4 Bxd4, White has a slight edge due to Black's bad bishop on c8.
notes.teaches: When the Greek Gift is not available, White can still regain the pawn and maintain pressure. The bishop on d3 remains active, and Black's French bishop is a long-term weakness.
notes.plans: Play h3 to prevent ...Qg5, then recapture on d4, followed by c3 to support the knight and leave Black with a passive bishop.

notes.explains: After d4 g6 e4 Bg7 Nc3 c6, Black has entered the Gurgenidze System, a hybrid of the Caro-Kann and Modern. White's main move is f4, but a practical alternative is Be3, reserving f3 for later.
notes.teaches: Delaying f4 in favor of Be3 is flexible: it develops a piece and keeps options open, while f3 can be played later to support the center and restrict Black's knight.
notes.plans: Play f3 next to build a strong pawn center, then develop queenside and prepare to castle long.

notes.explains: After …d5, the position resembles the Fantasy Variation of the Caro-Kann, but with White's knight on c3 and bishop on e3 already developed—both are ideal squares for that structure.
notes.teaches: When Black plays d5 in this system, White's setup (Nc3, Be3) fits naturally with the Fantasy plan: the bishop belongs on e3 and the knight on c3 in that variation.
notes.plans: Play f3 to support e4 and prepare to develop the kingside, then consider e5 or other central breaks.

notes.explains: With f3 played, White solidifies the center. Black's knight on g8 often struggles: Nh6 is met by Qd2 (protecting f5), and Nf6 runs into e5, forcing the knight to an awkward square like d7.
notes.teaches: In this structure, Black's knight development is problematic because natural squares (h6, f6) are easily punished. Delaying e5 keeps the knight out of play.
notes.plans: Continue developing, aiming for Qd2 and long castling, while keeping the option of e5 to harass Black's knight.

notes.explains: Black's …e5 opens the center prematurely. White is ahead in development, so blasting open lines favors the better-developed side. After dxe5, Black cannot play d4 because White has two defenders (Nc3, Be3) against one attacker.
notes.teaches: When your opponent opens the center while behind in development, you should welcome it. Always check if a central pawn push like d4 is possible—here it's impossible due to superior control.
notes.plans: Capture on e5, then consider capturing on d5 or developing with Qd2 and long castling.

notes.explains: After Qd2, Black cannot play d4 because the queen hangs with checkmate. If Black plays Nc6, White has Bb5, pinning the knight and indirectly defending d4. This tactical nuance makes Qd2 safe and effective.
notes.teaches: When calculating, always check if your opponent's pawn push is possible. Here, d4 is impossible due to the queen's alignment with the king. Also, pins can be used to indirectly defend key squares.
notes.plans: Continue with O-O-O, then bring the knight to d4 to blockade the IQP, and prepare kingside attack with h4 or g4.

notes.explains: Black plays Qd7, preparing queenside castling. White can continue improving with Kb1 (king safety) or Bb5 (pinning the knight). Both are good; the choice is a matter of taste and time management.
notes.teaches: When two moves are similarly good, don't spend excessive time deciding. Use intuition and time management; the decision is unlikely to decide the game.
notes.plans: Play Kb1 to secure the king, then continue with Rde1 or h4. Alternatively, Bb5 to pin the knight and prevent Nxd4.

notes.explains: White's Qxd4 is a poor move in the Sicilian because it loses tempi, essentially playing a Scandinavian Defense with colors reversed but with a pawn already on e4, which is worse for White.
notes.teaches: In the Sicilian, White should avoid early queen sorties that waste time; development and central control are paramount.
notes.plans: Black should attack the queen with Nc6, forcing it to move again, gaining time.

notes.explains: After …a5, Black prevents b4 but weakens b5. White's king is on d1, and the c5 pawn is hanging. The position is sharp; White must decide how to handle the extra pawn.
notes.teaches: When you have an extra pawn but your king is exposed, prioritize development and piece activity over clinging to the pawn at all costs. Look for flexible moves that create threats and improve your pieces.
notes.plans: Play Na3, aiming for Nb5, threatening Nc7+ and forcing concessions. If Black plays e6/e5, jump to b5 and then possibly d6, securing the bishop pair and dark-square control.

notes.explains: Na3 is a flexible developing move that prepares Nb5. It avoids immediate pawn defense and instead creates a threat (Nc7+) that forces Black to react. This is more effective than passive defense like Be3 or a3.
notes.teaches: When defending a weak pawn, indirect methods (creating threats) are often superior to direct defense. A knight on b5 can be a powerful outpost, especially when the black queen is gone.
notes.plans: Follow up with Nb5, then either Nc7+ or Nd6, depending on Black's response. If Black plays Nd5, consider Bc4 or c4 to challenge the knight.

notes.explains: Black plays Nd5, covering c7 but the knight is unstable. White has two good options: Bc4 (simple development, threatening to trade and secure the c5 pawn) or Nb5 (more aggressive, threatening c4 and Bc4). Nb5 is particularly strong because it forces Black to make concessions to defend c7.
notes.teaches: When a knight is on d5, it can be a target. Use pawn breaks (c4) or piece pressure (Bc4, Nb5) to challenge it. A knight on b5 creates a double threat (c4 and Nc7) that is hard to meet.
notes.plans: Play Nb5, threatening Nc7+. Black's best reply is Kd8, after which White can also consider Ng5, targeting f7. Alternatively, Bc4 is simpler and solid.

notes.explains: After Nb5 Kd8, Black has moved his king and cannot castle. White now has a strong initiative. Ng5 is a logical follow-up, hitting f7 and creating a double-knight attack on the kingside. Black must defend f7, often with g5, weakening further.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king has moved, double-knight attacks (Nb5 and Ng5) can be devastating. Don't be afraid to play aggressively; knights can retreat if needed.
notes.plans: Play Ng5, threatening Nxf7. If Black plays g5, then f4 can open lines. Alternatively, Bc4 is simpler and also strong.

notes.explains: Black plays Be6 to defend f7. White can immediately take on e6, ruining Black's pawn structure and creating doubled e-pawns. This is a permanent structural weakness for Black.
notes.teaches: When you have the chance to ruin the opponent's pawn structure with a capture, do it. Doubled pawns are a long-term liability, especially in the endgame.
notes.plans: Take on e6 with the knight (Nxe6), then develop the bishop to h3 or g4 to target the e6 pawn. The king can stay on d1 or move to e2.

notes.explains: After Nxe6 fxe6, Black has doubled e-pawns and a weak e6 pawn. White's king is safe on d1. The plan is to develop the bishop to h3 (via g3) to attack e6 and then bring the rook to d1, targeting the knight on d5.
notes.teaches: In positions with a structural advantage, focus on the weakest point. The e6 pawn is a target, but the immediate threat is the knight on d5, which can be attacked with Rd1.
notes.plans: Play g3, then Bh3, attacking e6. Then Rd1, threatening to win the knight on d5. If Black defends with Rd8, Nc7+ forks the rook.

notes.explains: g3 prepares Bh3, targeting e6. It also covers f4 and h4, restricting Black's knights. The move is more flexible than Be2-g4 because it also supports a future pawn push on the kingside.
notes.teaches: When choosing a development scheme, consider not only the immediate target but also the long-term control of squares. g3 and Bh3 is a prophylactic setup that also attacks.
notes.plans: Follow with Bh3, then Rd1. The threat of Rd1 is devastating because the knight on d5 has no good retreat and Black cannot castle.

notes.explains: Black plays e5, trying to free his position. White can simply take the pawn (Bxe5) because the bishop on h3 will prevent the black king from escaping to c8 after a check on d1.
notes.teaches: When the opponent tries to create counterplay, be ready to capture material if it doesn't weaken your position. The bishop on h3 serves a dual purpose: attacking e6 and controlling the c8 square.
notes.plans: Take on e5 with the bishop, then play Rd1+. The king will be forced to e8, and then Nc7+ wins the rook.

notes.explains: After the main moves, Black has several options: Bg4, e6, Nc6, and others. The position is highly theoretical. White's plan is flexible, often involving Na3 and Nb5.
notes.teaches: In the Alapin, White's setup is solid and flexible. The key is to develop quickly and target the c7 square with a knight on b5.
notes.plans: Against Bg4, consider h3 and then g4 to drive the bishop away. Against e6, play Na3 and Nb5. Against Nc6, dxc5 is strong.

notes.explains: After e4 c5 c3 d5 exd5 Qxd5 d4 Nf6 Nf3, we reach a key Alapin position. Black's queen on d5 is exposed, and White's c3 pawn supports d4 but blocks the knight's natural square. Black's best is Nf6, developing with a threat.
notes.teaches: In the Alapin, White's c3 pawn prepares d4 to occupy the center, but it also restricts the b1 knight. Black's queen on d5 is vulnerable to harassment, so Black should develop quickly rather than capture on d4 prematurely.
notes.plans: White aims to develop naturally, waiting for Black to commit. If Black plays e6, White can consider unusual knight maneuvers like Na3 to target b5 and c7.

notes.explains: Bg4 pins the knight. White can play h3, and if Bh5, then g4, forcing the bishop to retreat. This is a common idea to gain space and tempo.
notes.teaches: When your knight is pinned, don't be afraid to advance pawns to drive the bishop away. This can give you a space advantage and open lines.
notes.plans: Play h3, then g4, chasing the bishop to g6. Then develop with Nbd2 or Be2, and later target the f3 pawn if Black takes.

notes.explains: e6 is a solid move, preparing to develop the bishop. White's best is Na3, heading for b5. This is a standard plan in the Alapin.
notes.teaches: When Black plays e6, the knight on b5 becomes a powerful outpost. It threatens Nc7+ and forces Black to react.
notes.plans: Play Na3, then Nb5. If Black plays Qd8, then Qxd4 or Nxd4. If Black plays Na6, then White has a pleasant endgame.

notes.explains: Black plays e6, a solid move that prepares kingside development (Be7, O-O) and leaves the c8 bishop for later. White now has a choice: standard development or the aggressive Na3.
notes.teaches: Against e6, White's most promising plan is Na3, with three ideas: (1) Nb5 threatening Nc7 fork, (2) preparing Bc4 with tempo, and (3) if Black plays a6, Nc4 targets the weak b6 square.
notes.plans: White plays Na3, intending Nb5 or Nc4 depending on Black's response. If Black allows Nb5, White follows with Bf4 to pressure c7.

notes.explains: After dxc5 Qxd1+ Kxd1, White has an extra pawn but the king is in the center. Black's best is e5 or Bg4. The endgame is tricky but favorable for White due to the c5 pawn and better piece activity.
notes.teaches: Don't be afraid to enter an endgame with the king exposed if you have a pawn advantage and active pieces. The king can often find safety later.
notes.plans: Develop quickly, aiming to secure the c5 pawn or trade it for positional gains. Na3 and Nb5 is a common plan.

notes.explains: e5 is a common move, trying to challenge White's center. White should play b4, gaining space and threatening to develop with tempo. If Black plays e4, the knight can go to d4.
notes.teaches: When Black pushes e5, respond with b4 to gain space on the queenside. This is a typical Alapin idea.
notes.plans: Play b4, then develop the bishop to e3 or b5. The king can go to c1 or b2 for safety.

notes.explains: Bg4 pins the knight. White's best is Be3, developing and protecting the c5 pawn. If Black plays Nc5, then Bxc5 is possible, but the engine prefers Bc4.
notes.teaches: When Black pins the knight, develop the bishop to e3 to support the center and the c5 pawn. Be aware of tactical nuances like ...Nxe3 fxe3.
notes.plans: Play Be3, then consider h3 to drive the bishop away. If Black takes on f3, recapture with the pawn and use the open g-file.

notes.explains: Bd2 is a passive but recently popular move; White intends to recapture on c3 with the bishop to preserve queenside pawn structure.
notes.teaches: In the Nimzo-Indian, Black often trades the bishop for the knight on c3 to weaken White's control over e4.
notes.plans: Black will develop with b6, Bb7, d6, and Nbd7, creating a solid, flexible setup.

notes.explains: Black plays b6, preparing Bb7 and a solid setup. This is a standard Nimzo-Indian plan, avoiding d5 which would be less thematic.
notes.teaches: The Nimzo-Indian setup with b6, Bb7, d6, and Nbd7 is solid because it creates no weaknesses and gives Black easy development.
notes.plans: Continue with Bb7, d6, Nbd7, then consider either Qe7 followed by e5, or the more aggressive Ne4 and f5.

notes.explains: Black puts a knight on e4, a natural outpost. This is a typical idea in many openings, often followed by f5 to support the knight and start a kingside attack.
notes.teaches: A knight on e4 supported by f5 is a classic attacking structure; it pressures White and can lead to a kingside initiative.
notes.plans: After Ne4, play f5 to reinforce the knight and prepare further kingside expansion.

notes.explains: Black plays Ne4, the principled response, challenging the bishop immediately. White often replies h4 (Hodgson variation), intending to recapture with the h-pawn if Black takes on g5, opening the h-file and freezing Black's kingside pawns.
notes.teaches: In the Trompowsky, Ne4 is a sharp, principled move that forces White to commit. If White plays h4, Black should not take on g5, as that plays into White's plan.
notes.plans: Black should aim to undermine White's center and exploit the weakened kingside. A simple plan is to play d5, then retreat the knight to f6, reaching a solid Queen's Gambit Declined structure.

notes.explains: Black retreats the knight to f6 after provoking h4. White's extra tempo has been spent on a weakening pawn move, so Black's piece maneuver is justified. The position resembles a reversed Queen's Gambit Declined.
notes.teaches: Moving the same piece multiple times is acceptable if you provoke a weakness (like h4) and the center remains closed. The extra tempi spent by the opponent on weakening moves offset the loss of time.
notes.plans: Black will play e6 and then c5 to contest the center, exploiting White's passive development. The light-squared bishop can be developed later via d7 or b7.

notes.explains: White plays b4 to lure Black's c-pawn away from c5, aiming to occupy the center with d4. This gambit is dubious; Black can achieve an advantage with accurate play.
notes.teaches: In gambits, the key is to accept the pawn when it doesn't compromise your development, but be wary of moves that give White extra tempos.
notes.plans: Black should consider capturing with the pawn (cxb4) rather than the knight, to avoid allowing White to gain time with c3.

notes.explains: After cxb4, White typically plays d4. Black must avoid being overrun in the center. The immediate d5 by Black is natural, but it can lead to a queen sortie that White can harass.
notes.teaches: When facing a gambit, contesting the center early is crucial, but be careful not to expose your queen to attacks that lose time.
notes.plans: Black can play d5, but after exd5 Qxd5, White may play c4 attacking the queen. Black should be ready to retreat the queen or find a safe square.

notes.explains: Black plays d5, but this can lead to positions where White's pawns become powerful. An alternative is d6, which is more modest but avoids sharp theory and forces White to think for themselves.
notes.teaches: When you are unfamiliar with the theory of a sharp line, a solid, slightly inferior move can be a practical choice to avoid prepared lines.
notes.plans: After d6, Black aims to develop pieces and keep the center closed, preventing White's pawns from advancing too quickly.

notes.explains: Black plays d6, a modest move that prevents White's e-pawn from advancing easily. White has only one piece developed, so Black is not far behind in development.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a quiet move that stops the opponent's plans is better than a flashy one that opens lines for the opponent.
notes.plans: Black will develop the knight to f6, fianchetto the dark-squared bishop, and castle kingside, aiming to neutralize White's center later.

notes.explains: White develops the bishop to b2, eyeing the long diagonal. Black's pawn on d6 is a weakness, but Black should not play f6 as it hinders development.
notes.teaches: Avoid weakening pawn moves that impede your piece development. Instead, focus on developing with threats.
notes.plans: Black should play Nf6, attacking e4 and forcing White to react. This is a natural developing move that also creates counterplay.

notes.explains: Black plays Nf6, attacking the e4 pawn. White may respond with Qd4, attacking the knight and the g7 pawn. Black must be careful not to lose the g7 pawn.
notes.teaches: When your opponent threatens multiple things, prioritize the most dangerous threat. Here, defending g7 is crucial to avoid king-side collapse.
notes.plans: Black should retreat the knight to f6 (or possibly d6) to defend g7. Then continue development with g6 and Bg7.

notes.explains: Black captures on d4, opening the c3 square for White's knight. White refrains from the tempting Bc4 because of Qe4+; instead, Nb5 is the correct intermezzo, threatening Nc7 fork.
notes.teaches: When a fork is threatened, do not automatically recapture. Look for intermediate moves that maintain or increase the threat. Here Nb5 is stronger than Bc4 because it keeps the fork alive.
notes.plans: After Nb5, Black must defend c7. If Black plays Bd6, White can respond with Bc4, exploiting the pin on the d-file and threatening to win material.

notes.explains: White plays Be3, a patient developing move that maintains the pressure. Black's queen on e4 is vulnerable, and the bishop on d6 is still hanging due to the fork threat. White will recapture on d4 after Black deals with the threats.
notes.teaches: Patience in attack is crucial. Instead of forcing immediate tactics, complete development while maintaining threats. Be3 is both developing and keeps the pressure on Black's disorganized pieces.
notes.plans: White will soon recapture on d4 with the knight, gaining a huge lead in development. Black's king is stuck in the center, and White's pieces coordinate perfectly.

notes.explains: Black plays Ke7, a desperate move to unpin the bishop and avoid the fork. White now has the simple Nxd6, winning the bishop pair and driving the king to d6, where it remains exposed.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, exchanging to win the bishop pair is often strong. The king on d6 is a permanent target, and White's lead in development becomes decisive.
notes.plans: White plays Nxd6+ Kxd6, then Nxd4, threatening Nf5+ and a devastating attack. Black cannot take on g2 due to Nf5+ leading to mate.

notes.explains: White recaptures on d4 with the knight, threatening Nf5+. Black's king on d6 is a sitting duck. White now castles to unpin the bishop and bring the rook into play.
notes.teaches: After winning material, consolidate by castling and activating rooks. Do not rush for a knockout; instead, improve your position and let the opponent's weaknesses tell.
notes.plans: White castles, then plays Re1 to harass the queen and open the e-file. The immediate threat is Nf5+, but White must first unpin the bishop on e3.

notes.explains: Black plays e5, hoping to dislodge the knight. White responds with Bg5, pinning the knight on f6 and forcing the queen to move. The queen has few safe squares that keep contact with e5.
notes.teaches: When the opponent tries to create counterplay, use pins and threats to maintain pressure. Bg5 is strong because it forces the queen away while also pinning the knight.
notes.plans: After Bg5, Black's queen must move to g6 or g4. White then captures on e5, forcing the king back to f8, followed by Ne6+ forking the rook on d8 and leading to mate.

notes.explains: Black played ...Ba6 to attack the c4 pawn, but this was a mistake. The correct move was ...Bb7, which supports a central break with ...d5 after ...exf5. With the bishop on a6, ...d5 is less effective because White can reply Ng5, threatening f6 and creating a strong attack.
notes.teaches: When choosing a square for a bishop, consider how it supports your central pawn breaks. Compare ...Ba6 vs ...Bb7: the latter directly supports ...d5, while the former leaves the center vulnerable.
notes.plans: Black should have played ...Bb7, then after ...exf5, play ...d5 to open the center and activate the pieces.

notes.explains: Black's Nd4 is a premature centralization. With only one developed piece, Black cannot have a real trick here.
notes.teaches: A piece in the center is not automatically good if it lacks support and can be attacked. When the opponent has few developed pieces, you can safely capture pawns without fear of traps.
notes.plans: Capture on e5, then retreat the knight to f3 to attack Black's knight and consolidate the pawn.

notes.explains: Retreating Nf3 kills two birds: it moves the knight to safety and attacks Black's knight on d4. Black immediately blunders by exchanging knights, leaving White up a piece.
notes.teaches: When you are up material, simplify by trading pieces. Avoid unnecessary complications.
notes.plans: Develop naturally, complete kingside development, and then convert the material advantage.

notes.explains: After d4 Nf6 Nc3 d5 Bf4, White has set up the Jobava London. Black's most common response is ...e6, but White's immediate threat is Nb5, targeting c7. Black has three main defenses: ...Bb4, ...Na6, and ...Bd6. The most popular on Lichess is ...Bd6, which is actually the worst of the three.
notes.teaches: In the Jobava London, White often plays for a quick Nb5 to pressure c7. Black's most common reply is often suboptimal, so knowing the correct responses gives White an edge.
notes.plans: After ...Bd6, White can play e3 and then develop naturally, aiming to exploit Black's passive bishop placement.

notes.explains: After d4 Nf6 Nc3 d5 Bf4 Bf5 e3 e6 Nf3 Nbd7, Black's setup looks solid but is deceptive. White can immediately play g4, threatening h5 to trap the bishop on f5. If Black plays ...h6, White takes on f5, ruining Black's pawn structure and leaving the g6 pawn weak.
notes.teaches: In the Jobava London, the g4-h5 pawn advance is a common tactical idea to trap Black's light-squared bishop or destroy Black's kingside pawn structure.
notes.plans: After g4, if Black plays ...h6, White takes on f5 and then plays Qf3, pinning the king and threatening g5, with a winning attack.

notes.explains: After d4 Nf6 Nc3 d5 Bf4, if Black plays ...Nc6, White has a winning tactic: Nb5! Black cannot defend c7 adequately. Similarly, ...Nbd7 also loses to Nb5.
notes.teaches: In the Jobava London, ...Nc6 and ...Nbd7 are immediate losing moves due to the threat of Nb5 attacking c7. Always be alert for such tactical shots.
notes.plans: Play Nb5, threatening Nxc7+ and winning material.

notes.explains: Black offers a pawn with e5, hoping to lure White into natural moves that lead to traps. Accepting the pawn is correct.
notes.teaches: Always accept gambit pawns unless there is a concrete refutation; do not pre-move on move 1.
notes.plans: Take on e5 and prepare to meet Black's responses.

notes.explains: After dxe5, Black's main moves are Nc6, Qe7, d6, f6, and Bc5. Each requires a specific response.
notes.teaches: Know the key responses to each of Black's second-move alternatives to avoid falling into traps.
notes.plans: Respond to Nc6 with Nf3; to Qe7 with Bg5 (main line); to d6 with Nf3; to f6 with e4; to Bc5 with Nc3.

notes.explains: Black plays f6, trying to open lines. White should meet this with e4, indirectly defending the e5 pawn.
notes.teaches: When Black attacks the gambit pawn with f6, counter with e4 to maintain the pawn and prepare development.
notes.plans: After e4, if Black plays Nc6, continue with Nf3 and Bc4, aiming for a Fried Liver Attack style.

notes.explains: After Nf3, Black's best is fxe5, but then Bc4 gives White a powerful attack similar to the Fried Liver, with Black's king stuck in the center.
notes.teaches: Sacrificing back the gambit pawn can lead to a devastating attack if Black's king is exposed.
notes.plans: Play Bc4, then Ng5, threatening forks and checks. If Black plays Nf6, continue with Ng5, aiming for Bf7+ and Qh5+.

notes.explains: Black plays d6, aiming to transpose to lines with Nc6. White should play Nf3, and if Nc6, continue with Bg5.
notes.teaches: Against d6, develop naturally and use Bg5 to force Black into a weak pawn structure.
notes.plans: After Nf3 Nc6, play Bg5. If Black plays Bb7, trade and take on d6, leaving Black with an isolated d-pawn and no compensation.

notes.explains: This is the main line. Black's Qe7 threatens Qb4+ forking the bishop and king. White should play Bg5, walking into the trap.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you must allow the opponent's threat to refute the gambit; Bg5 invites Qb4+, but White has a strong response.
notes.plans: After Bg5, if Qb4+, play Nc3, then after Qxb2, Bd2, and follow the queen sacrifice line.

notes.explains: Black takes the pawn on b2. White's Bd2 protects the knight and prepares to trap the queen. Black's best is Bb4.
notes.teaches: When the queen is deep in enemy territory, use piece development to trap it or gain time.
notes.plans: After Bb4, play Rb1, then if Qa3, Nd5; if Qxc3, Bxc3 Bxc3, then Nd2, and White has queen for two pieces with an attack.

notes.explains: Black plays Qa3, avoiding immediate loss. White should play Nd5, centralizing the knight and threatening further attacks.
notes.teaches: Centralize your pieces; a knight on d5 is powerful and restricts Black's options.
notes.plans: After Nd5, if Bxd2+, Qxd2; if Ba5, e4, then develop kingside and use Rb3 or Bc1 to trap the queen or attack the king.

notes.explains: Black trades bishops. White recaptures with the queen, maintaining the initiative. Black's king is stuck in the center.
notes.teaches: After a queen trade, White's development advantage and Black's weak king often lead to a winning attack.
notes.plans: Play e4, then develop the kingside with Be2 or Bc4, castle, and aim for Ng5 or Qg5 to attack Black's king.

notes.explains: Black plays Ba5, keeping the tension. White should play e4, then develop with Be2 and castle, preparing Rb3 and Bc1.
notes.teaches: Patience is key; develop naturally and use retreating moves like Bc1 to trap the queen or create threats.
notes.plans: After e4, play Be2, castle, then Rb3, and if the queen moves to a4, Bc1 followed by Bd3 and Rb3 to trap it.

notes.explains: White plays e4, solidifying the center and preparing development. Black's pieces are cramped.
notes.teaches: A strong pawn center restricts the opponent's pieces and provides a base for attacks.
notes.plans: Develop the kingside with Be2, castle, then use Rb3 and Bc1 to target Black's queen or launch a kingside attack.

notes.explains: Black develops the knight. White should play g4, a powerful novelty that prepares g5 and Bg2, putting pressure on Black's position.
notes.teaches: Use pawn storms to open lines against the opponent's king, especially when you have a material advantage.
notes.plans: Play g4, then Bg2, g5, f4, castle, and Ne4, creating a crushing attack. If Black castles, continue with the pawn storm.

notes.explains: g4 is a key move. It prepares g5 to drive away the knight and Bg2 to control the long diagonal.
notes.teaches: In positions with a queen for two pieces, use your pawns to create threats and open lines.
notes.plans: Follow up with Bg2, then g5, f4, castle, and Ne4. If Black plays d5, play g5 anyway, then trade pieces and continue the attack.

notes.explains: Black takes the a2 pawn. White should play Rd1, building pressure on d7. Black's best is Kd8.
notes.teaches: When the opponent grabs a pawn, use the tempo to improve your piece activity and create threats.
notes.plans: After Rd1, if Kd8, play e4, then develop with Be2 or Bc4, castle, and aim for Ng5 or Qg5 to attack the king.

notes.explains: Black's king moves to d8. White should play e4, then develop the kingside and castle.
notes.teaches: Even when the opponent's king is safe for now, continue developing and prepare a kingside attack.
notes.plans: Play e4, then Be2 or Bc4, castle, and then use Ng5 or Qg5 to create threats. If Black plays Nge7, chase it with h4 and h5.

notes.explains: White plays e4, solidifying the center. Black is paralyzed; White can develop at leisure.
notes.teaches: A strong center and development advantage can leave the opponent with no good moves.
notes.plans: Develop with Be2, castle, then play Ng5 or Qg5, targeting f7 and h7. If Black tries to trade queens, avoid it and keep the pressure.

notes.opening: Italian Game, Fried Liver Attack, Traxler Counterattack
notes.explains: Black plays Bc5 instead of the main move d5, leaving f7 undefended. This is a serious gambit, not a blunder.
notes.teaches: The Traxler Counterattack is a dangerous opening that requires precise play from White. Do not assume it is a mistake.
notes.plans: White must avoid the natural capture Nxf7, which leads to wild complications. Instead, consider the move d4.

notes.opening: Italian Game, Fried Liver Attack, Traxler Counterattack
notes.explains: Black's only good response to d4 is d5, counterattacking the bishop. White should take with the bishop: Bxd5.
notes.teaches: When your opponent plays a counterattack, you must be precise. Taking with the bishop is best here.
notes.plans: After Bxd5, Black has several tries, but White can force a favorable endgame or maintain a pawn-up advantage.

notes.opening: Italian Game, Fried Liver Attack, Traxler Counterattack
notes.explains: If Black takes on d5 with the knight, White should take the bishop on c5, not the knight. This forces a favorable endgame.
notes.teaches: In complex tactical positions, sometimes the best move is to simplify into a winning endgame rather than continue the attack.
notes.plans: After Bxc5, Black's knight is misplaced, and White is up a pawn with a better structure.

notes.opening: Italian Game, Fried Liver Attack, Traxler Counterattack
notes.explains: If Black plays Nxd4 instead of taking on d5, White plays Bxf7+ Kxf7, and Black's attack fizzles after careful play.
notes.teaches: When the opponent sacrifices material for an attack, you can often return the material to consolidate.
notes.plans: White can play c3 to kick the knight, then develop and castle, remaining a pawn up.

notes.opening: Italian Game, Fried Liver Attack, Traxler Counterattack
notes.explains: After Bxf7+ Ke7, White retreats the bishop to c4, threatening Nf7 and preparing c3 to kick the knight on d4.
notes.teaches: In the Traxler, White's plan is to force the black king to e7, then consolidate with c3 and development.
notes.plans: White will play c3, forcing the knight back, then develop with Be3, O-O, and enjoy a pawn-up position.

notes.opening: Italian Game, Fried Liver Attack, Traxler Counterattack
notes.explains: Black's best try is b5, attacking the bishop. White retreats to d3, and the position remains favorable.
notes.teaches: When under attack, retreating to a safe square is often better than trying to hold ground.
notes.plans: White will continue with c3, kicking the knight, then develop and castle. Black's activity is temporary.

notes.opening: Italian Game, Fried Liver Attack, Traxler Counterattack
notes.explains: If Black plays h6, White retreats the knight to f3, not fearing the pin. The knight is well-placed on f3.
notes.teaches: Don't be afraid of pins if you can easily break them. Here, the knight on f3 is safe and supports the center.
notes.plans: White will play Nbd2, then possibly castle or drop the bishop back to e2. Black's attack is illusory.

notes.opening: Italian Game, Fried Liver Attack, Traxler Counterattack
notes.explains: If Black plays Rf8, White plays c3, forcing the knight back. Black has no real threats.
notes.teaches: In the Traxler, Black's rook on f8 does not create enough pressure. White can simply kick the knight and consolidate.
notes.plans: After c3, White can trade pieces and enjoy a pawn-up endgame with a safe king.

notes.opening: Italian Game, Fried Liver Attack, Traxler Counterattack
notes.explains: If Black plays Bg4, White responds with f3, forcing the bishop to retreat. Then c3 kicks the knight.
notes.teaches: f3 is a useful move in this line to break the pin and gain space. Don't be afraid of weakening the kingside.
notes.plans: After f3 and c3, White's position is solid and Black's attack is over. White can then develop and win.

notes.opening: Italian Game, Fried Liver Attack, Traxler Counterattack
notes.explains: Black's best move is Qe8, preparing Qg6. White plays Nbd2, and if Qg6, then c3 counterattacks the knight.
notes.teaches: In complex positions, counterattacking the opponent's pieces can be more effective than passive defense.
notes.plans: After c3, if Black takes on g5, White trades queens and wins material. If the knight moves, White develops and remains better.

notes.explains: White sacrifices the f-pawn to gain central control and facilitate d4. The immediate d4 is a mistake because it allows Qh4+ and forces the white king to move.
notes.teaches: The King's Gambit is not refuted; Black must know precise responses. The main idea is to prevent Qh4+ by playing Nf3 first.
notes.plans: White aims to win back the pawn with Bc4 or d4 after Nf3, while Black seeks to hold the pawn and counterattack.
